contract-authoring/psl-syntax: PSL, the Prisma Schema Language, is the preferred way to author your contract, the contract.prisma file that replaced schema.prisma . You usually write one file, src/prisma/contract.prisma , or split it into several, and npx prisma contract emit writes contract.json and contract.d.ts beside it. If you know the Prisma schema language, most of a contract file reads exactly as you expect. The five biggest additions are listed here, and the rest of the page is the full reference for every attribute and block mixins write a set of fields, attributes or enum members once and include it in several blocks. named types give a database column type a name you can reuse on many fields. enums an enum can now say how its values are stored, and what each member stores. value objects a structured value stored inside its parent row, with no table of its own. base models and variants one table can hold more than one kind of record. Put the shared fields in a base model, put the differences in each variant, and Prisma ORM uses one column to tell them apart. extension types field types that come from an npm package, such as vectors. The datasource and generator blocks are gone the connection URL and the file paths are set in prisma.config.ts instead. Coming from Prisma ORM 7 lists every change to the schema file, including what each old @db. attribute becomes. A complete contract The first non blank line of every contract file is // use prisma 8 , because contract emit reads only the .prisma files that start with it. When the contract setting in prisma.config.ts names one file and that file lacks the line, contract emit fails with CONTRACT.SOURCE LOAD FAILED , and the error's details include PSL NO OPTED IN SCHEMA FILES . When contract is a glob that matches several files, a file without the line is left out of the contract without a warning, and contract emit fails only when none of the files has it. Uuid is PostgreSQL's uuid type written as a field type. Run npx prisma contract emit after any change to refresh contract.json and contract.d.ts , and then npx prisma db init creates the tables. Point the config at the schema The config's contract path names the file Prisma ORM reads. If the path ends in .prisma , Prisma ORM reads it as PSL, and if it ends in .ts , as TypeScript. The db key holds the connection URL npx prisma orm init writes a config like this, DATABASE URL included. The import chooses the database @prisma/orm postgres/config makes it a PostgreSQL project, and @prisma/orm mongo/config a MongoDB one. Coming from Prisma ORM 7 lists the other keys. Split the contract across several files Set contract to a glob, such as "./src/prisma/ / .prisma" , to write the contract in several files. Every matching file that starts with // use prisma 8 becomes part of one contract, and a file you add later joins it on the next contract emit , with no change to the config. A model in one file can refer to a model in another. contract emit writes contract.json and contract.d.ts into the folder before the first wildcard, here ./src/prisma/ . See Configuration. Models and fields Models declare fields with a type, an optional ? marker, and attributes. Scalar fields lists the types a field can hold, among them String , Int , Boolean , Decimal , DateTime , Json , and Bytes . On PostgreSQL, Int , BigInt , Float , Decimal , String , Boolean and Bytes are convenience types, named for what the field means. Each becomes one explicit type, which is named after the database type and sets the column and the kind of value your code reads. Written bare, each gives the type in the first row for it below. For Int , BigInt , Float and String , the storage argument chooses another column. Decimal , Boolean and Bytes have only the one column shown. as chooses what your code reads from a BigInt Written Becomes Column Your code reads Int Int4 int4 a number Int(storage int2) Int2 int2 a number BigInt Int8BigInt int8 a bigint BigInt(as number) Int8Number int8 a number ; a read or write outside the safe integer range fails BigInt(storage numeric) NumericBigInt numeric a bigint of any size Float Float8 float8 a number Float(storage float4) Float4 float4 a number Decimal NumericString numeric a decimal string String Text text a string String(storage varchar) Varchar varchar a string String(storage char) Char char a string Boolean Bool bool a boolean Bytes Bytea bytea a Uint8Array Decimal also takes precision and scale , and String with storage varchar or storage char takes length , as in Decimal(precision 10, scale 2) and String(storage varchar, length 35) . Write these three by name, because a positional argument fills storage first Decimal(10, 2) is refused at storage . String(length 35) is refused too, because a bare String is a text column, which has no length. The contract stores only the explicit type, so you can also write the explicit type itself, such as Int2 , Varchar(35) or NumericString(10, 2) . You can also use one of these PostgreSQL types as the field type Uuid , Inet , Bit , Varbit , Xml , Oid , Money , or one of the date and time types below. Bit(8) and Varbit(64) set a length, and TimestamptzTemporal(3) or DateTime(precision 6) sets how many digits of a second are kept. Write each length, precision and scale as a whole number without quotes Varchar("35") and Varchar(35.0) are refused with PSL VALUE TYPE INCOMPATIBLE . Xml reads and writes text and has no equality, so no filter can compare it. Oid reads a whole number from 0 to 4294967295. Money reads a decimal string with two fraction digits, such as " 1234.56" , whatever the database's locale. The names SmallInt , BigIntNumber , Numeric , UnboundedInt , Real , VarChar and VarBit are deprecated. They still work and give the same contract, but contract emit and the editor report the warning PSL DEPRECATED SCALAR NAME where one is written, and they will be removed. Write the convenience type that gives the same type instead. VarBit has no convenience type, so write the explicit type Varbit Deprecated Write instead SmallInt Int(storage int2) BigIntNumber BigInt(as number) Numeric(10, 2) Decimal(precision 10, scale 2) UnboundedInt BigInt(storage numeric) Real Float(storage float4) VarChar(12) String(storage varchar, length 12) VarBit(16) Varbit(16) On PostgreSQL, a date or time field is written with one of four types named for what the field means. Each becomes one explicit type, which names the column and the kind of value your code reads. At their defaults they need no Temporal Written Becomes Column Your code reads DateTime TimestamptzJsDate(3) timestamptz(3) a JavaScript Date Date DateString date a string, such as "2024 02 29" Time TimeString time a string, such as "09 30 00" Duration IntervalString interval an ISO 8601 duration, such as "P1M" Arguments choose another explicit type. as picks what your code reads jsDate , string or temporal for DateTime , string or temporal for Date and Time , and string or parts for Duration . storage picks the column timestamptz or timestamp for DateTime , and time or timetz for Time . precision sets the digits of a second. So DateTime(as temporal) is TimestamptzTemporal , read as a Temporal.Instant ; DateTime(as string) is TimestamptzString ; DateTime(storage timestamp) is TimestampJsDate(3) ; Date(as temporal) is DateTemporal , a Temporal.PlainDate ; Time(as temporal) is TimeTemporal , a Temporal.PlainTime ; Time(storage timetz) is Timetz ; and Duration(as parts) is IntervalParts , read as { months, days, micros } . The contract stores only the explicit type, so you can also write the explicit type itself. TimestampTemporal , a timestamp read as a Temporal.PlainDateTime , has no convenience form. A type read as a Temporal value needs a global Temporal , and Scalar fields says how to check for it. The string types are ISO 8601 on every server, whatever its TimeZone and DateStyle a timestamptz reads as the instant in UTC, such as 2024 01 01T00 00 00Z . The exception is infinity and infinity , which PostgreSQL can store in a date or timestamp column a string type reads them as infinity and infinity , and a type read as a Date or a Temporal value fails to read them with RUNTIME.DECODE FAILED . A JavaScript Date holds milliseconds, so a type read as a Date on a column with more digits of a second, such as DateTime(precision 6) , drops the rest. TimestampJsDate and TimestampInstant read a timestamp column as a Date and a Temporal.Instant , treating the stored date and time as UTC. @id marks the primary key. @@id([a, b]) declares a composite key. @unique adds a unique constraint on one field. @@unique([userId, title]) adds one across several fields. @@index([...]) declares a secondary index. @default(...) sets a database default the database fills in the column when an insert leaves it out. The default is a literal, now() , autoincrement() , or any other SQL expression. Write the SQL as a sql tagged literal, which is sql followed by the SQL in backticks, such as @default(sql gen random uuid() ) . See Default values for how to write each kind of literal. @onCreate(...) sets a value Prisma ORM generates when it creates the row, and @onUpdate(...) one it generates on every update. See Generated values. @map("column name") sets a field's column name in the database. @@map("table name") sets the table or collection name when it differs from the model name. Without @@map , the table or collection has the model's name exactly as written, so model UserProfile is the table "UserProfile" . @@check(expression sql total = 0 , name "order total positive") adds a check constraint of your own to the table. See Check constraints. @@control(observed) says how far Prisma ORM manages the table. See Control policy. A field can be a list on PostgreSQL tags String[] is a text[] column, and the same works for Int[] and the other scalar types. Prisma ORM adds a check constraint to a list column so it cannot hold a NULL element. To allow NULL elements, put the ? on the element type String?[] allows null elements, String[]? allows a null list, and String?[]? allows both. In your code, String?[] is a ReadonlyArray , String[]? is a ReadonlyArray null , and String?[]? is a ReadonlyArray null . A String?[] column has no check constraint, so use it for a list column that already exists without one. A list of an enum or of a named type works the same way, and so does a list of a value object, as Value objects shows. How IDs map differs by database On PostgreSQL the primary key is an ordinary column, so pick its type and default yourself. On MongoDB the primary key is the document's id , so type it ObjectId and map it to id . Your code still names the field id , in rows, where , select , orderBy , and write data @map changes only the name in the stored document. A field of a value object cannot take @map , because it is always stored under its own name. Generated values @onCreate(fn()) and @onUpdate(fn()) name a function that Prisma ORM runs in your application to fill the field @onCreate when it creates the row and you leave the field out, @onUpdate on every update. The functions are uuid() , a version 4 UUID, the same as uuid(4) , and uuid(7) , a version 7 UUID. cuid(2) , ulid() , and ksuid() . nanoid() , 21 characters long, and nanoid(n) , n characters long, from 2 to 255. now() , the current time. Each function makes a value for the field's type uuid() works on String , Varchar(n) , Char(n) , and Uuid , and now() works on every PostgreSQL date and time type, Date , Time , and Timetz included. The database does not fill these columns, so a row written by raw SQL or another application gets no value. A field may have both a database @default and an @onCreate(...) createdAt DateTime @default(now()) @onCreate(now()) takes its time from your application when Prisma ORM creates the row, and from the database for other inserts. On an optional field, @onCreate(...) fills the field when you leave it out, and an explicit null is stored as null . @onUpdate(...) alone generates nothing on create. If a required field has @onUpdate(...) and no @onCreate(...) or @default , you must pass a value for it in ORM create and upsert . To have it generated on create too, add @onCreate(...) . @default(uuid()) and the other functions that generate a value are refused in @default with PSL GENERATOR IN DEFAULT , which names the @onCreate(...) to write. @default(now()) and @default(autoincrement()) stay they are database defaults. An argument a function does not take, such as uuid(5) , cuid(1) , or nanoid(300) , is refused with PSL INVALID GENERATOR ARGUMENT , and cuid() needs its version, cuid(2) . An argument written with a fraction, such as nanoid(8.0) , or in quotes, is refused with PSL VALUE TYPE INCOMPATIBLE . The value a function writes must also fit its column uuid() writes 36 characters, ksuid() 27, ulid() 26, cuid(2) 24, nanoid() 21, and nanoid(n) n , so String(storage varchar, length 5) @onCreate(uuid()) is refused when you run contract emit . A bare Char holds one character, and a varchar without a length has no limit. For the column of a generated identifier, write its type alias. UuidString , Ulid , Nanoid , Cuid2 and Ksuid are Char(36) , Char(26) , Char(21) , Char(24) and Char(27) , as in id Ulid @id @onCreate(ulid()) . The alias sets only the column, so the field writes @id and @onCreate(...) itself, and a foreign key that holds the identifier uses the alias alone, as in authorId Ulid . On SQLite, write the aliases in the sql namespace, such as sql.Ulid , and a fixed length text column as sql.Char(n) . On PostgreSQL a new schema can store a UUID in the native Uuid column instead, as id Uuid @id @onCreate(uuid(7)) . note[Upgrading from before 8.0.0 rc.21 ] Field presets, such as id.ulid() , nanoid({ size 12 }) , json() and temporal.updatedAt() , are removed. prisma contract emit refuses each one with PSL UNRESOLVED REFERENCE , and the message gives the exact rewrite, such as Ulid @id @onCreate(ulid()) , Char(12) , Jsonb or temporal.UpdatedAt . Each rewrite stores the same contract as the preset did before 8.0.0 rc.22 . Since 8.0.0 rc.22 , temporal.UpdatedAt is a timestamptz(3) column read as a Date , where temporal.updatedAt() read a Temporal.Instant , so follow the upgrade instructions for those fields that came out with that release. Prisma ORM 8 has no @updatedAt . To replace @updatedAt , write updatedAt temporal.UpdatedAt Prisma ORM sets the field to the current time on every create and update, and you can still set it yourself on a write. temporal.CreatedAt sets its field once, when the row is created. You do not import or declare temporal it is a group of named types built into the contract syntax. On PostgreSQL the column is timestamptz . Both take the time from your application's clock, not from the database, so the column has no database default, and a row you insert with raw SQL must supply the value. For a value the database generates, use DateTime @default(now()) instead. temporal.UpdatedAt is written without parentheses. It is DateTime @onCreate(now()) @onUpdate(now()) , a timestamptz(3) column your code reads as a JavaScript Date , and temporal.CreatedAt is DateTime @onCreate(now()) . Write the attributes yourself for another type or a precision, such as DateTime(as string) @onCreate(now()) @onUpdate(now()) for a string. The example at the top of this section writes them on a DateTime field only to show the attributes. now() takes the column's precision and rounds the time down to it, so the value a create returns is the value PostgreSQL stores. A field written with as temporal , such as DateTime(as temporal) @onCreate(now()) , needs a global Temporal for writes as well as reads. When your Node.js version has none, install temporal polyfill and add import "temporal polyfill/full/global" at the top of src/prisma/db.ts . Columns of any database type For a column of a database type no field type covers, write Raw(sql ... ) with the type written the way the database reports it. To see that text for a column that already exists, run prisma db schema Migrations create the column with that text, and db verify compares it with the type the database reports, so write integer , not int4 , and quote a name that needs it, as in Raw(sql "MyType" ) . Your code reads and writes the value as unknown , and a default is a sql tagged literal. Raw("ltree") , without the sql tag, is refused. Raw works on PostgreSQL and on SQLite, which Prisma ORM 8 supports as an experimental package. Default values Write each default in a form its column can hold. A quoted string is text, for example, so it cannot be the default of a JSON, decimal, or floating point column. When a default does not fit its column, contract emit fails with PSL VALUE TYPE INCOMPATIBLE , pointing at the value you wrote, and the message says what to write instead, such as Expected a number . A single value on a list field fails with PSL DEFAULT LIST EXPECTED , and text that is not a valid value of its kind, such as a json literal that is not a JSON document, fails with PSL INVALID LITERAL . The examples below show the form for each kind of column A JSON default is a json tagged literal json followed by the JSON document in backticks. Write a JSON array the same way, as tags shows. A decimal default is a bare number. NaN , Infinity , and Infinity are written without quotes, and so are true and false . A text default is a quoted string. A fixed date, time, or interval is a tagged literal named after the column's PostgreSQL type timestamptz for DateTime and the other timestamptz types, and timestamp , date , time , timetz , and interval for the types of those names, as in @default(interval P1D ) . A timestamptz default is a point in time with a UTC offset, such as timestamptz 2024 01 01T00 00 00Z , and a timestamp default has no offset, such as timestamp 2024 01 01 00 00 00 . A quoted string on one of these fields is refused, and the message shows the tagged literal to write. A Bytes default is a bytea tagged literal holding the bytes as hexadecimal after \x , as payload shows. Base64 text is not accepted. On SQLite, a DateTime default uses the datetime tag, as in @default(datetime 2024 01 01T00 00 00Z ) , and a Bytes default the blob tag, which holds hexadecimal digits, as in @default(blob 68656c6c6f ) . Each default, and each member of an enum , is checked by the column's type, so a value the column cannot hold unchanged is refused more characters than a varchar(n) or char(n) column takes, a number a numeric(p, s) column would round, more digits of a second than a TimestamptzTemporal(3) keeps, digits below a millisecond on a field read as a JavaScript Date , which cannot hold them (also on MySQL's DateTime ), an integer outside the range of Int or Int(storage int2) , or text that is not a UUID on a Uuid field. A date or time default that the field's type does not hold makes contract emit fail with PSL INVALID DEFAULT LITERAL , and the message shows a text the field takes. That includes an offset on a timestamp , date , or time default, a missing offset on a timestamptz or timetz default, more than six digits after the decimal point (three on SQLite), and a date or time that does not exist, such as 2024 02 30 . The CLI checks these defaults on Node.js 24 too, which has no built in Temporal . On a field typed with an enum block, the default is the member's name without quotes, as in @default(Low) . On a pg.enum(...) field, it is the value the member stores, in quotes, as in @default("admin") . Enums covers both. Any other SQL expression is a sql tagged literal, and it goes into the column default exactly as written. Write the current time as now() and a sequence as autoincrement() , not as sql now() or sql autoincrement() , which are refused. Prisma ORM 7's dbgenerated("...") is not accepted, and contract emit reports PSL UNKNOWN DEFAULT FUNCTION . Write the same SQL as a sql tagged literal instead, so @default(dbgenerated("gen random uuid()")) becomes @default(sql gen random uuid() ) . contract infer writes every default in these forms. Indexes @@index([...]) takes a list of fields, and on PostgreSQL the named arguments below. Either the list or expression is required, and an expression index needs a name expression is the whole index expression as SQL, in place of the field list. where makes a partial index; it is the condition as SQL, without the WHERE keyword. unique makes a unique index. @@unique([...]) is a unique constraint, which is the usual way to say a value must be unique; use unique on @@index when you also need expression or where . type picks the index method, such as "hash" or "gin" . name names the index. The name in the database is not exactly what you typed it gets an eight character hash on the end, user name active 000a85d8 , and if you change name later, the next migration plan renames the index instead of dropping and recreating it. map instead sets the exact name, for an index that already exists in the database, which is what contract infer writes for indexes it finds. Give one or the other, not both. Advanced PostgreSQL shows when each kind of index is the right one. expression and where take a sql tagged literal, as @default does; a quoted string there is refused with PSL VALUE TYPE INCOMPATIBLE . Inside the literal no quote is escaped, and it may span lines. Prisma ORM stores the SQL with its shared indentation and the blank lines at its start and end removed. The SQL goes into the database as written, so it uses column names, not field names (they differ when a field has @map ), and you quote the names yourself. Prisma ORM does not check the SQL until the migration runs. On MongoDB, @@index takes different arguments; see MongoDB indexes. Full text indexes @@fullTextIndex([...]) creates the GIN index that PostgreSQL full text search uses. It takes one or more text fields, and it needs either name or map , but not both Each top level item of the list is a weight group, strongest first, and an item can itself be a list of fields that share a weight. In post search , a match in title or subtitle ranks above a match in body . An index takes one to four groups, a group cannot be empty, and a field can appear only once. In an index of several fields, Prisma ORM wraps every column in coalesce(column, '') , so the index does not change when a column becomes optional or required. language sets the text search language, which tells PostgreSQL how to break the text into searchable words. It defaults to english , and you set it as in @@fullTextIndex([title], name "post title search", language "german") . where makes it a partial index, as on @@index . A field typed pg.enum(...) , a PostgreSQL enum type as Enums describes, cannot have a full text index. PostgreSQL only. To search an index, name it in the query fns.fullTextMatches(indexes.post search, q) in an ORM where callback, as Full text search shows. The query then reads the index's fields, weights and language from the contract, so it searches exactly what the index covers and PostgreSQL can use the index. For a partial index, made with where , PostgreSQL uses it only when the query's own where also implies the index's condition, so add that condition to the query and check the plan with EXPLAIN . You can also search one text field with its own fullTextMatches and fullTextRank functions, as in p.title.fullTextMatches(query, { language "german" }) ; give that search the same language as the index, because PostgreSQL does not use the index for a search in another language. Check constraints @@check adds a check constraint you write yourself, on top of the ones Prisma ORM generates for enum and list columns expression is the condition as a sql literal, using column names, as on @@index . name and map work as they do on @@index name for a constraint you are adding, and map for one that already exists in the database under that exact name. A model can carry any number of @@check attributes. PostgreSQL only. Prisma ORM also adds two check constraints of its own one on every enum column, so it accepts only the enum's values, and one on every list column, so it rejects NULL elements. A list whose elements may be NULL is written T?[] , and it gets no check, as Models and fields describes. Control policy @@control(...) says how far Prisma ORM manages the table, with one of four values Value db verify Migrations managed (the default) The table must exist and match the model exactly. Create, alter, and drop it. tolerated Declared columns must match; extra columns are accepted. Create it if missing; never alter or drop it. external Declared columns must match; extra columns and constraints are ignored. Never touch it. observed Anything goes; a mismatch is a warning, not a failure. Never touch it. Put it on a model whose table something else owns, such as an audit table another system writes Mixins A mixin is a named set of members you write once and include in several blocks. Declare it with the block's keyword followed by mixin , and include it with + and its name The contract is the same as if the mixin's members were written where the + line is, so User has the fields id , createdAt , updatedAt and email , in that order, and the index on createdAt , and Role has the members ADMIN , USER and GUEST . A model mixin goes only in models, a type mixin only in composite types, an enum mixin only in enums, and a mixin for a block an extension adds, such as policy select mixin , only in blocks of that keyword. A field or enum member that the block already has, from its own body or from another mixin, is an error, and so is including the same mixin twice in one block. A mixin's own attributes can name only its own fields, as @@index([createdAt]) does. A model's attributes can name the fields a mixin gives it, as in @@id([tenantId, id]) . A mixin cannot include another mixin, and it is not a type, so it cannot be a field's type. A mixin declared in namespace auth { } is included from another namespace as +auth.Timestamps , and the types of its fields are looked up in auth . The language server completes mixin names after + , and goes to, hovers, renames and colors them. Named types The types block gives a database column type a name you can reuse on many fields Fields then use ShortName like any built in type. The name keeps the column decision in one place a varchar(35) column rather than text . You do not have to name a type a field can use the type directly, such as String(storage varchar, length 35) , Decimal(precision 10, scale 2) , Uuid , or TimestamptzTemporal . A named type is shorthand the contract stores the column type, not the name. A named type can also set @default , @onCreate and @onUpdate , and every field typed by it gets them. In this example, TimestampString(3) is a PostgreSQL timestamp(3) column that your code reads as a string @id and @unique belong to a field, not to a type, so write them on the field, as slug does. On a named type they are refused with PSL UNSUPPORTED NAMED TYPE ATTRIBUTE . A field may add any attribute its named type does not set. Here updatedAt adds @default(now()) , a database default, so a row inserted outside Prisma ORM also gets a time. A field that repeats an attribute its named type already sets is refused with PSL DUPLICATE ATTRIBUTE . A named type is built on a type or an enum, not on another named type. Prisma ORM provides two named types you do not declare temporal.CreatedAt , set to the current time on create, and temporal.UpdatedAt , set on create and on every update. Write them without parentheses, as createdAt does above. On PostgreSQL they store a timestamptz(3) column that your code reads as a JavaScript Date . They take no arguments. For a string, a Temporal value or a precision, write the type and the attributes yourself, such as DateTime(as string) @onCreate(now()) @onUpdate(now()) , as UpdatedAt above does. Each form of BigInt gives your code a different kind of value Type Column In your code BigInt bigint a JavaScript bigint BigInt(as number) bigint a JavaScript number ; a read or write outside the safe integer range fails BigInt(storage numeric) numeric a JavaScript bigint of any size In Prisma ORM 8 the field's type sets the column, so String @db.VarChar(35) from Prisma ORM 7 becomes String(storage varchar, length 35) , and the @db. attributes are gone. The types block works on PostgreSQL, SQLite and MongoDB. On MongoDB a named type cannot set @default , because MongoDB has no database defaults; MongoDB data modeling covers the differences. Enums An enum lists its members, and with @@type it can also say how their values are stored and what each member stores In pg/text@1 , pg is PostgreSQL, text is the column type, and @1 is the version of how the value is stored and read. Write @@type("pg/int4@1") to store the values as integers instead. When a member has no explicit value, the member name itself is stored. Each member's value is a value of the enum's type, written as a @default of that type is a quoted string for text, a bare number for a number type, and a tagged literal for a date or time. A quoted member on a number type, such as Half = "0.5" under @@type("pg/numeric@1") , is refused, and the message shows what to write, here Half = 0.5 . Two members may not store the same value. Prisma ORM compares the values, not the text you wrote, so on pg/numeric@1 the members 0.5 and 0.50 store the same value and are refused. On MongoDB the same rule applies, with MongoDB's types. A quoted member is text ( mongo/string@1 ), and true and false are booleans. Write a number bare, NaN and the infinities included, and a date or binary value with its tag, as in date 2024 01 01T00 00 00Z or binary aGVsbG8= These members are refused A quoted member on a type that does not take text, such as Unknown = "NaN" under mongo/double@1 . The error is PSL VALUE TYPE INCOMPATIBLE , and its message says what to write. A mongo/int32@1 or mongo/int64@1 member written with
contract-authoring/editor-support: Install the Prisma VS Code extension to get error checking, formatting, and completion in your .prisma file. In Prisma ORM 8 that file is the data contract the description of your models that Prisma ORM 7 called the schema. Its path is the contract setting in your prisma.config.ts , which is prisma/contract.prisma in the config orm init writes; see Configuration. Coming from Prisma ORM 7? Start with Coming from Prisma ORM 7. This page covers VS Code only. The file header The extension only works on .prisma files whose first non blank line is A file without that line gets no error checking, no completion, and no formatting. prisma contract emit also skips it without a warning, and when none of the files that the contract setting names has the line, contract emit fails with CONTRACT.SOURCE LOAD FAILED . orm init and contract infer write the line for you. Add it yourself when you create a contract by hand. What the editor does Errors appear inline as you type. They are the same errors you would get from prisma contract emit , the command that checks the contract and writes contract.json and contract.d.ts . Formatting reformats the whole file. In VS Code, run Format Document . Completion starts when you type @ or @@ . The editor lists attribute names such as @id , @default , and @@index , each with a short description. Inside an attribute, it lists the names of the arguments you have not filled in yet and suggests values for them. It also suggests values inside [ ] and { } . In a MongoDB index's field list, it suggests the option and its values in the parentheses after a field name, such as sort and Desc in @@index([createdAt(sort Desc)]) . Where an attribute expects a field name, it suggests only scalar fields. When an attribute has required arguments, VS Code inserts them as placeholders named after each argument, which you tab through. In a block such as policy select , it completes the values, including inside lists and function calls, and offers ns. for a namespace. A block value can name an entity in another namespace, as in target = auth.Account . Hover shows what a name is. Over a model, field, type, or block, it shows the declaration and its /// doc comment. Over an attribute, argument name, function, constant, or a type from an extension pack, it shows the signature and its documentation. Go to definition jumps from a use of a name to its declaration, and Find references lists every place a name is used. Both work for models, composite types, named types, blocks, fields, and namespaces, across every file of the contract. Signature help appears when you type ( or , inside an attribute. It shows the attribute's arguments and describes the one you are typing. The list of attributes comes from your prisma.config.ts the database it declares and the Prisma extension packs listed under extensions ; see Extension packs for that config. Extension packs are add on packages for database features such as pgvector. If your config lists the pgvector pack, the editor also suggests pgvector's attributes. No database connection is needed. A contract in several files When contract in prisma.config.ts is a glob, such as ./ .prisma , the editor reads every matching file that starts with // use prisma 8 as one contract, the same files that prisma contract emit reads. A model declared in a file you have not opened is known in the files you edit, and the editor reports the errors in every file of the contract, including the ones you have not opened. See Split the schema across several files. False errors after an upgrade If the editor marks attributes as errors in a contract that prisma contract emit accepts, the likely cause is an old ORM package. That is the @prisma/orm postgres , @prisma/orm mongo , or @prisma/orm sqlite package your project installs for its database. Check the installed version If it prints a version below 8.0.0 rc.9 , update it to the latest version Replace orm postgres with orm mongo or orm sqlite to match your database. Then reload the editor window. In VS Code, run Developer Reload Window from the Command Palette.
contract-authoring/typescript-schema-bui: In Prisma ORM 8, schema.prisma is replaced by a file called the contract, which holds the model definitions you used to write in schema.prisma . You can write it in two forms one is a .prisma file written in PSL, short for Prisma Schema Language, and the other is TypeScript, in src/prisma/contract.ts , built with the defineContract builder. Both forms produce the same two files npx prisma contract emit writes contract.json and contract.d.ts into the folder that holds your contract file. When to choose TypeScript over PSL PSL is the preferred way to write the contract, and both forms produce the same two files, so you give up nothing by staying with PSL. Use the TypeScript builder for the cases PSL does not cover, and reach for it when model definitions must be split, composed, or reused across ordinary TypeScript modules or packages you want to build models in a loop from data you already keep in TypeScript, such as one model per entry in a list of table names If neither applies, write PSL, which is more compact and is what contract infer writes. Point the config at the contract file For a new project, run npx prisma orm init , which asks how you want to write your schema, and choosing TypeScript creates the contract file and the config together. The config's contract path names the one file Prisma ORM reads, and a .ts extension selects TypeScript authoring. An optional output names a directory for contract.json and contract.d.ts , which otherwise land next to the contract file; npm create prisma@latest sets it to ./src/prisma/generated for TypeScript projects A complete contract The builder comes from your database's package @prisma/orm postgres/contract builder for PostgreSQL, @prisma/orm mongo/contract builder for MongoDB. Export the contract under the name contract , as below, or as the file's default export, because those are the only two names prisma contract emit looks for. Run npx prisma contract emit again after every edit to the contract, and commit the contract file together with contract.json and contract.d.ts . How defineContract works On PostgreSQL, defineContract takes an options object and then a function. You do not set a provider anywhere importing @prisma/orm postgres/contract builder is what selects PostgreSQL. The options object lists the extension packs you use, and you write {} when you use none. The function returns the contract's content models , plus enums and entities if you have them. There is no types key defineContract refuses one with CONTRACT.TYPES KEY REMOVED . Write a type alias as a constant instead, as Type aliases shows. The options object takes four more keys, all optional Option What it does naming { tables "snake case", columns "snake case" } Derives table and column names from model and field names, so createdAt becomes created at without a .column(...) call on every field. Set either key or both. foreignKeyDefaults { constraint true, index true } Gives every rel.belongsTo a foreign key constraint and an index in the database. Without this option a relation gets neither unless its own .sql({ fk }) asks; see Relations. defaultControlPolicy "managed" The control policy for every model that does not set its own. namespaces ["audit"] The PostgreSQL schemas other than public that models may use; see Namespaces. Take field , model , rel , type , and gen from the function's one argument, because those include the helpers your extension packs add, and import defineContract , enumType , and member from the package. The package also exports model , rel , field , and gen . Use those only in code outside the function, and expect them to lack the extension packs' helpers. On MongoDB, defineContract also accepts a single object holding models , as above, and you import field , model , and rel from the package instead. The type of that object is ContractInput , which you import from @prisma/orm mongo/contract builder , as on SQL. A model of the built contract is a ContractModel , with ContractModel from @prisma/orm mongo/contract/types and MongoModelStorage from @prisma/orm mongo/family contract . The MongoDB builder differs from the PostgreSQL one in how it handles the primary key, field helpers, collection names, relations, indexes, and validators The field stored as id is always the primary key, so you never mark it with .id() and there is no .attributes(...) on MongoDB. Declare it as id field.objectId().mongo({ field " id" }) to name it id in your code, as id ObjectId @id @map(" id") does in PSL, or as id field.objectId() to keep the name id . .mongo({ field }) sets the name a field is stored under in its documents, for any field of a model. A model without an id field gets one from MongoDB, an ObjectId, on every insert. The scalar helpers are field.objectId() , field.string() , field.int32() , field.double() , field.bool() , and field.date() . The collection name is an inline option on the model rather than a chained call, and relations are inline as well. Relations name the field on each side. rel.hasMany takes { from, to } on MongoDB and { by } on PostgreSQL. to accepts either the field name as a string or a typed reference such as User.ref("id") , and both forms mean the same thing. PostgreSQL writes that reference as User.refs.id . Indexes are an indexes option on the model, built with the index helper the same package exports, as in indexes [index({ email 1 }, { unique true })] . The 1 is ascending, MongoDB's own index syntax. Each collection gets a $jsonSchema validator built from its model, as with a PSL contract, so MongoDB refuses a document with a field the model does not declare, a missing required field, or a value of the wrong type. defineContract refuses what a validator cannot describe, such as an id field that is optional or a list. To keep a collection without a validator, give its model controlPolicy "observed" . Enums and extension packs work on MongoDB too enumType and member come from @prisma/orm mongo/contract builder . Pass the enums in the same object as the models, as defineContract({ models, enums }) , and extension packs go in the same extensions option. The contract records its packs, so pass each pack's runtime to the client too, as mongo({ contract, url, extensions [myPack] }) , or the client fails with RUNTIME.MISSING EXTENSION PACK . Every enum a field uses must be in enums , including an enum that types a field of a value object; an enum that is missing fails with CONTRACT.ENUM UNKNOWN . defineContract , a PSL contract and a Prisma ORM 6 schema read with prisma6Schema all build a MongoDB contract the same way, so the rules below apply to each of them. The exception is indexes prisma6Schema keeps them as Prisma ORM 6 wrote them, with the names Prisma ORM 6 gave them, such as User email key , and merges none of them. The MongoDB builder also has, on the model object indexes , a list of index(keys, options?) calls. keys maps each field to 1 , 1 , "text" , "2dsphere" , "2d" , or "hashed" , and options takes MongoDB's own index options unique , sparse , name , expireAfterSeconds , partialFilterExpression , collation , weights , and wildcardProjection . For example, index({ expiresAt 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds 3600, sparse true }) . An index MongoDB would refuse fails with CONTRACT.INDEX INVALID a unique wildcard index, a wildcard with a hashed, 2d or 2dsphere key, a hashed index on several fields, a wildcard index with expireAfterSeconds , a wildcardProjection without a wildcard key, a collation without a locale , and a second text index in one collection. Each index is named after its keys and their directions, such as email 1 , unless its name option sets one, and migrations create and drop each index by that name. Two index(...) calls with the same keys, options and name give one index, counting an option set to false as left out, and a plain index beside a unique one with the same keys and otherwise the same options gives the unique index alone. Other indexes of one collection that get one name fail with CONTRACT.NAME DUPLICATE , because MongoDB cannot hold both. Two indexes with the same keys and options but different names fail with CONTRACT.NAME DUPLICATE too. Remove one, or give both the same name so they become one index. A unique and a sparse index on email are both named email 1 , for example, so name one of them indexes [index({ email 1 }, { unique true }), index({ email 1 }, { sparse true, name "email sparse" })] . Upgrading from before 8.0.0 rc.23 gives every MongoDB contract with an index a new storage hash; MongoDB indexes lists the steps, which update the migration snapshots and then run prisma db sign or apply a migration with no operations. collectionOptions , for options on the collection itself, such as { collation { locale "en", strength 2 } } . discriminator and base , for one collection that holds more than one kind of document. The base model declares discriminator { field "kind", variants { Article { value "article" } } } , and each variant model declares base Post plus its own fields. A variant is stored in its base's collection, so leave its collection out or set it to the base's; another collection fails with CONTRACT.COLLECTION INVALID . The discriminator must be a required field.string() or a string enum, every variant it lists must be a model declared with that base, and each variant's value must be a value the discriminator can hold. A variant field must not be stored under a name a different base field uses ( CONTRACT.NAME DUPLICATE ). A variant may restate a base field under the same name only if it declares it exactly as the base does. MongoDB data modeling covers when to use it. And two more field helpers field.vector() for a vector, which takes no dimension count, and field.valueObject(Address) for an embedded document, where Address is declared with valueObject("Address", { fields { ... } }) from the package and returned in defineContract 's valueObjects map The examples below use the PostgreSQL builder. Fields A field is field.column(...) with a type from type , the function's other argument. type has a helper for every type PSL can write. On PostgreSQL Column Field text field.column(type.String()) integer field.column(type.Int()) big integer field.column(type.BigInt()) float field.column(type.Float()) decimal field.column(type.Decimal()) boolean field.column(type.Boolean()) date and time field.column(type.DateTime()) date field.column(type.Date()) bytes field.column(type.Bytes()) JSON, stored as jsonb field.column(type.Jsonb()) UUID stored in a uuid column field.column(type.Uuid()) UUID stored in a character(36) column field.column(type.UuidString()) On PostgreSQL, type.DateTime() , type.Date() , type.Time() and type.Duration() are the convenience date and time types. Each takes one optional object with the keys its PSL type takes as , storage and precision for type.DateTime() , type.Time() and type.Duration() , and as for type.Date() , such as type.DateTime({ as 'string' }) or type.Time({ precision 3 }) . type.Int() , type.BigInt() , type.Float() , type.Decimal() , type.String() , type.Boolean() and type.Bytes() are the convenience types for numbers, text, booleans and bytes, and take their PSL arguments in the same way, such as type.Int({ storage 'int2' }) , type.BigInt({ as 'number' }) , type.Decimal({ precision 10, scale 2 }) or type.String({ storage 'varchar', length 64 }) . The other helpers take the arguments their PSL types take, such as type.Varchar(64) , type.NumericString(10, 2) and type.TimeTemporal(3) . field.column(type) and the chained .column(...) below are different calls field.column(type) builds a field from a type, and .column(name) on an existing field sets its column name. Extension packs add helpers of their own, such as type.pgvector.Vector(1536) . type.SmallInt() , type.BigIntNumber() , type.Numeric(...) , type.UnboundedInt() , type.Real() , type.VarChar(...) and type.VarBit(...) are deprecated, like their PSL names. They still compile, and nothing warns where they are called, but they will be removed together with the PSL names. Call the convenience helper that gives the same type instead, such as type.String({ storage 'varchar', length 64 }) for type.VarChar(64) , or type.Varbit(16) for type.VarBit(16) , which has no convenience helper. For a column of a database type no helper covers, use type.Raw(sql ... ) , with the type written the way the database reports it, as in path field.column(type.Raw(sql ltree )) , with sql imported from the package. It works as Raw(sql ... ) in PSL does your code reads and writes the value as unknown , and a default is a sql expression. To generate a value in your app on any field, chain .onCreate(...) with a call from gen , and .onUpdate(...) to generate one on every update. gen has gen.uuid() , gen.uuid(7) , gen.cuid(2) , gen.ulid() , gen.nanoid() , gen.nanoid(16) , gen.ksuid() , and gen.now() , the same functions as @onCreate and @onUpdate in PSL, and each makes a value for the field's column type For a primary key your app generates, chain .id() and .onCreate(...) , as id does above. On PostgreSQL the native uuid column is the best choice for a new contract. For an identifier stored as text, type has an alias for the column of each format type.UuidString() , type.Ulid() , type.Nanoid() , type.Cuid2() and type.Ksuid() are type.Char(36) , type.Char(26) , type.Char(21) , type.Char(24) and type.Char(27) . The alias sets only the column, so write the generator yourself, as in field.column(type.Ulid()).id().onCreate(gen.ulid()) , and give a foreign key that holds the identifier the alias alone, field.column(type.Ulid()) . On SQLite the aliases are in the sql namespace, such as type.sql.Ulid() , and a fixed length text column is type.sql.Char(n) . A field may have both field.column(type.DateTime()).default(now()).onCreate(gen.now()) takes its time from your app when Prisma ORM creates the row, and from the database for other inserts. .onUpdate(...) alone generates nothing on create. If a field that is not .optional() has .onUpdate(...) and no .onCreate(...) or .default(...) , you must pass a value for it in ORM create and upsert , as for field.column(type.TimestamptzTemporal()).onUpdate(gen.now()) . To have the field generated on create too, add .onCreate(...) . For a key the database generates, chain .default(...) and .id() on a field. An integer that counts up is field.column(type.Int()).default(autoincrement()).id() , and a UUID is field.column(type.Uuid()).default(sql gen random uuid() ).id() . Import autoincrement and sql from @prisma/orm postgres/contract builder . field.column(type.temporal.CreatedAt()) sets the column to the current time when the row is created, and field.column(type.temporal.UpdatedAt()) sets it on every create and every update. Prisma ORM sets both in the client, from your application's clock, so the column has no database default. If you insert a row with raw SQL, you must supply the value yourself. For a time the database sets instead, use field.column(type.DateTime()).default(now()) , with now imported from @prisma/orm postgres/contract builder . On PostgreSQL, type.DateTime() , type.temporal.CreatedAt() , and type.temporal.UpdatedAt() are timestamptz(3) columns that give your code a JavaScript Date , and need no Temporal . For a string or a Temporal.Instant , write the type and the generators yourself, such as field.column(type.DateTime({ as 'temporal' })).onCreate(gen.now()).onUpdate(gen.now()) . A type read as a Temporal value needs a global Temporal ; Scalar fields says how to check for it and which polyfill to load when it is missing. field.namedType(x) takes only an enum, as Enums shows. note[Upgrading from before 8.0.0 rc.21 ] The field presets are removed field.text() , field.uuidString() , field.json() and the other scalar presets, every field.id. , every field.temporal. , and field.generated(...) . TypeScript reports a missing property, and prisma contract emit on a contract that was not type checked fails with CONTRACT.FIELD HELPER UNKNOWN , which names the rewrite. Write each one as field.column(type.X(...)) with .id() , .onCreate(gen.fn()) and .onUpdate(gen.fn()) field.id.ulid() is field.column(type.Ulid()).id().onCreate(gen.ulid()) , and field.temporal.updatedAt() is field.column(type.temporal.UpdatedAt()) . Each replacement stores the same contract as the preset did before 8.0.0 rc.22 . Since 8.0.0 rc.22 , type.temporal.UpdatedAt() is a timestamptz(3) column read as a Date , where field.temporal.updatedAt() read a Temporal.Instant , so follow the upgrade instructions for those fields that came out with that release. On MongoDB, field.temporal.createdAt() is field.date().onCreate(gen.now()) , and field.date() , field.string() and the other MongoDB helpers stay. Type aliases type has a helper for every type PSL can write, such as type.Varchar(64) , type.TimestampString(3) and type.String() , plus type.temporal.CreatedAt() and type.temporal.UpdatedAt() , which work as temporal.CreatedAt and temporal.UpdatedAt in PSL do. PSL writes these without parentheses, while TypeScript calls them. Pass the result to field.column(...) . A type alias, the types { ... } block of PSL, is a constant in TypeScript. Field builders never change once built, so one constant serves every field and model that uses it, and a field can chain more onto it Each column stores the alias's type itself, as it does in PSL, so contract.json has no Slug . Chaining a generator the constant already sets, as in UpdatedAt.onUpdate(gen.now()) , throws CONTRACT.DEFAULT INVALID with reason generator phase set twice (you called .onCreate() or .onUpdate() twice). note[Upgrading from before 8.0.0 rc.20 ] A contract that returned a types map and used field.namedType(types.X) now fails with CONTRACT.TYPES KEY REMOVED . Replace each entry with a constant const X = field.column(type.Y(...)) , use the constant as the field, and remove types from the returned object. Then rewrite the contracts stored in migrations/ 1. From the project root, run node /scripts/expand type aliases/expand type aliases.ts . Node.js 24 or later runs the TypeScript file directly. 3. Run npx prisma contract emit . 4. Run npx prisma db sign db once for each database, with that database's connection string. The storage hash changes, but the database does not. Every field builder supports chained modifiers .optional() makes the field nullable. .default(value) sets a fixed default, written as a value of the type your code writes to the field. Fixed defaults below shows each kind. .default(...) also takes a default the database computes .default(now()) , .default(autoincrement()) , or any other SQL expression as a sql template, such as .default(sql gen random uuid() ) . Import now , autoincrement , and sql from @prisma/orm postgres/contract builder . sql now() and sql autoincrement() are refused, so use the named helpers. .defaultSql(expression) still works but is deprecated, and it will be removed in the stable 8.0.0 release. A field has one default. .default(...) on a builder that already has one, such as a type alias constant with a default, throws CONTRACT.DEFAULT INVALID with reason default set twice . .unique() adds a unique constraint. .id() marks the primary key, for a key that is not generated, such as an integer you set yourself. .column("column name") sets the column name in the database when it differs from the field name. .many() makes the field a list, stored as a PostgreSQL array column such as text[] . A list column gets a check constraint that rejects NULL elements. To allow NULL elements, write .many({ elementsNullable true }) the field's TypeScript type becomes ReadonlyArray . Add .optional() to allow a NULL list as well. .onCreate(gen.uuid()) and .onUpdate(gen.now()) generate a value in your app, as described above. Fixed defaults A fixed default passed to .default(value) has the type your code writes to the field A decimal default is a string .default("1.50") . A JSON default is the object or array itself .default({ plan "free" }) . A type.DateTime() default is a Date .default(new Date("2024 01 01T00 00 00Z")) . A type.DateTime({ as 'temporal' }) default is a Temporal.Instant . To write the time as a string instead, use field.column(type.TimestamptzString()).default("2024 01 01T00 00 00Z") . A type.BigInt() default is a bigint .default(1n) . A value of the wrong type is a type error in your editor. A value the column's type cannot hold makes contract emit fail with CONTRACT.DEFAULT INVALID , and a Temporal default with digits below one microsecond is refused too, as is a default with digits below a millisecond on a field read as a Date . Do not write .default(null) , because when you leave out an .optional() field that has no default, the database already stores NULL . Enums enumType declares an enum, the type its values are stored as, and its members, as Priority does in the full example above. The second argument says how each member is stored, as the codecId note in the full example above explains. Write as const after the object, so TypeScript keeps the exact string. To store the members as integers, pass { codecId "pg/int4@1" } as const . Write each member's stored value as the column stores it the column's type checks it, and defineContract refuses a value that type does not take with CONTRACT.ENUM INVALID . More type ids are listed with the raw query param helper, which names types the same way. Each member(name, storedValue) pairs the TypeScript visible name with the value stored in the column. Fields reference the enum with field.namedType(Priority) , and defaults reference a member as Priority.members.Low . Include the enum in the returned enums map so it reaches the two files. At runtime, db.enums holds each member as a query returns it, such as a bigint for pg/int8@1 . Members are stored in whatever column type you name here, text above. For a real PostgreSQL enum type, declare it with nativeEnum and type the field with pg.enum , both exported by @prisma/orm postgres/contract builder . The type is created in the database under the name you give it Role does not go in the returned enums map using it on a field is enough to create the type in the database. Relations Relations are declared on the model builder with .relations(...) and the rel helpers, as the full example above shows. rel.hasMany(Model, { by }) names the foreign key field on the other model, and rel.hasOne(Model, { by }) is the same with at most one row on the other side. rel.belongsTo(Model, { from, to }) maps the local foreign key field to the field it points at. rel.manyToMany(Model, { through, from, to }) goes through a join table you declare the model for the join table yourself and pass it as through . Below, PostTag is that model, holding the two foreign key fields postId and tagId rel.belongsTo on its own does not create a foreign key constraint in the database, so ask for one by chaining .sql(...) on the relation itself, inside the .relations({ ... }) object, as the full example above does fk takes name , onDelete , and onUpdate . onDelete and onUpdate each take 'noAction' , 'restrict' , 'cascade' , 'setNull' , or 'setDefault' . Prisma ORM does not check that the column types on the two sides of a relation match, so choose a field helper that produces the same column type as the key you point at. rel.hasMany , rel.hasOne , rel.belongsTo , and rel.manyToMany also accept the model name as a string. Pass the model object, as above, and a typo is a compile error, but pass a string and the typo is reported when prisma contract emit builds the contract. Storage mapping .sql(...) maps a model to its table, and the object form covers the common case User.sql({ table "user" }) . Without a table , and without the naming option, the table has the model's name exactly as written, so User is the table "User" . You can chain .relations(...) , .attributes(...) , and .sql(...) in any order, and you can skip any of them, so a model with no relations calls .sql({ table }) straight after model(...) . The callback form gives you the model's columns as cols and the constraint builders as constraints . Use it for indexes constraints.index takes a list of columns, even when the list has one entry, or an object with expression , the whole index expression as a sql value. The options are unique , where (a partial index condition as a sql value, without the WHERE keyword), type with options (the index method and its parameters; options {} when there are none), and name or map . name "user handle active" creates an index called user handle active 2a0c4277 , with a hash on the end; map sets the exact name, which is what you want when the index already exists. An expression index needs one of the two where and expression take a sql value, written with the sql tag from @prisma/orm postgres/contract builder , as .default() does; a plain string there is a type error. The SQL goes into the database as written, so it uses column names, and you quote them yourself. Prisma ORM stores it with its shared indentation and the blank lines at its start and end removed. A sql value can hold another sql ${owner} AND deleted at IS NULL joins the two texts, and anything else inside ${} is a type error. The primary key, unique constraints, indexes, and foreign keys of one model must all have different names. A name used twice is a type error that your editor and tsc report, but npx prisma contract emit does not type check the file, and it accepts the repeated name because each name gets a different hash on the end in the database. A map used twice makes contract emit fail with CONTRACT.SOURCE LOAD FAILED . For PostgreSQL full text search, fullTextIndex from @prisma/orm postgres/contract builder creates the GIN index that the fullTextMatches and fullTextRank query functions use. It takes one text column, or a list of weight groups as @@fullTextIndex does, such as [[cols.title, cols.subtitle], cols.body] , and a name or map , plus optional language and a where written as a sql value language defaults to english on both the index and the query functions, and PostgreSQL uses the index only when the two match, so change both or neither. To search German text, for example, write fullTextIndex(cols.title, { name "post title search", language "german" }) on the index and p.title.fullTextMatches(query, { language "german" }) in the query. Two more keys go in the same object, in either the object form or the callback form checks , a list of check constraints you write yourself, built with check from the package, and control , the model's control policy expression is the condition as a sql value, using column names, and name and map work as they do on an index. Model.refs provides typed references to another model's fields, for the constraint builders inside .sql(...) . Write constraints.foreignKey(cols.userId, User.refs.id) and TypeScript checks id against the actual User definition. For a primary key made of two fields, use .attributes(...) instead of .sql(...) , and build it from the field references That object accepts exactly two keys, id and uniques . id takes one constraint, and uniques takes a list, so uniques [constraints.unique([fields.postId, fields.tagId])] makes a unique constraint across two fields. For a key made of one field, .id() on the field is enough. Namespaces A model can go in a PostgreSQL schema other than public declare the schema in defineContract 's namespaces option, then name it on the model. Without the declaration, npx prisma contract emit fails and names the missing entry. Control policy control on .sql(...) says how far Prisma ORM manages the table, with one of four values Value db verify Migrations "managed" (the default) The table must exist and match the model exactly. Create, alter, and drop it. "tolerated" Declared columns must match; extra columns are accepted. Create it if missing; never alter or drop it. "external" Declared columns must match; extra columns and constraints are ignored. Never touch it. "observed" Anything goes; a mismatch is a warning, not a failure. Never touch it. Put it on a model whose table something else owns defaultControlPolicy in defineContract 's options sets the policy for every model that does not set its own. Row level security The package exports the pieces of PostgreSQL row level security, and migration plan turns them into ENABLE ROW LEVEL SECURITY and CREATE POLICY statements. rlsEnabled(Model) turns row level security on for the model's table. policySelect , policyInsert , policyUpdate , policyDelete , and policyAll each declare one policy for one operation, and role("name") declares a database role a policy names. Return them all in the entities list roles lists role handles, and a role you declare with role(...) goes in entities as well, as authenticated does above. Listing it there only names it, because Prisma ORM never creates or drops a role create it yourself, and db verify fails when it is missing. A role PostgreSQL always has, such as public , is role("public") in roles and left out of entities . using and withCheck are the two conditions as sql values, using column names policySelect and policyDelete take using , policyInsert takes withCheck , and policyUpdate and policyAll take either or both. The policy name gets an eight character hash on the end in the database. Extension types An extension pack is an npm package that adds column types to the builder. List packs in defineContract 's options object, and the type helper exposes their constructors List every pack whose column types the contract uses, also when you pass one of its types to field.column(...) .
