extensions: An extension is an npm package that adds something Prisma ORM does not do on its own a column type such as a vector or a geometry, an index type, query operations (new functions you can call in a query, such as pgvector's cosineDistance ), or middleware, which runs your own code before and after every query. To use PostgreSQL you install @prisma/orm postgres , and to use MongoDB you install @prisma/orm mongo , because support for a database comes from an extension too. Installing the package is not the whole job, because you register an extension in two places. It goes in prisma.config.ts , so that the command line tools know about it, and in db.ts , the file where you create the client, so that your queries can use what it adds. @prisma/orm postgres is the package you call directly ormConfig(...) in prisma.config.ts and postgres(...) in db.ts . Other extensions are listed in the extensions array passed to those two calls. Using extensions shows both registrations, with the install command, for pgvector. Middleware is the exception, because you register it on the client only, and How middleware works covers that. Your contract is what Prisma ORM 8 calls your schema contract.prisma in place of schema.prisma . If you have a Prisma ORM 7 project, Coming from Prisma ORM 7 says what replaced schema.prisma , @prisma/client , and $use . Catalog The extension directory has the install command and the registration snippet for each entry below. MySQL's library, @prisma/orm mysql , is an early preview for migrations, reads and writes, and Supported databases says what it covers and what is planned. An entry marked experimental works today, but its API can change between releases. {/ extensions catalog start /} Name What it adds Package Databases By arktype json JSON columns validated by an arktype schema and typed end to end. @prisma/orm extension arktype json PostgreSQL Prisma Cache middleware Serve repeated reads from an in memory or pluggable cache, opted in per query. @prisma/orm extension middleware cache PostgreSQL, MongoDB Prisma MongoDB MongoDB support for Prisma ORM config, runtime, contract authoring, BSON values, and migrations in one package. @prisma/orm mongo MongoDB Prisma ParadeDB (experimental) BM25 full text search ranked by relevance, with fuzzy, phrase, and proximity queries. @prisma/orm extension paradedb PostgreSQL Prisma pgvector Vector columns and similarity search for embeddings. @prisma/orm extension pgvector PostgreSQL Prisma PostGIS Geometry columns and geospatial queries such as distance and containment. @prisma/orm extension postgis PostgreSQL Prisma PostgreSQL PostgreSQL support for Prisma ORM config, runtime, contract authoring, and migrations in one package. @prisma/orm postgres PostgreSQL Prisma SQLite (experimental) SQLite support for Prisma ORM config, runtime, contract authoring, and migrations in one package. @prisma/orm sqlite SQLite Prisma Supabase (experimental) Supabase auth and storage tables plus role bound clients for row level security. @prisma/orm extension supabase PostgreSQL Prisma IndexedDB (experimental) Prisma 8 for IndexedDB a browser database from your PSL schema, with typed accessors and explicit migrations. @prisma idb/client idb IndexedDB Yash Kolekar typed json Typed JSON and text columns with no validator dependency. prisma orm extension typed json PostgreSQL Omar Dulaimi zod json Typed JSON columns described and enforced by a zod schema. prisma orm extension zod json PostgreSQL Omar Dulaimi {/ extensions catalog end /} Three of these have their own page PostGIS, ParadeDB, and arktype json. Using extensions walks through pgvector. In the Supabase row, role bound clients are client instances pinned to a particular PostgreSQL role, so the database applies that role's row level security policies to whatever you query through them. Publish your own An extension you write yourself is an npm package with one entry point for the command line tools and one for your application. Name your two entry points control and runtime , as pgvector does and as the call for extension authors describes. Middleware ships a single entry point instead, because it is only ever registered on the client. Name the package prisma orm , or @your scope/prisma orm if you publish under your own npm scope. List the keyword prisma orm extension in its package.json , so that people and tools searching npm can find every community Prisma ORM 8 extension To write middleware, follow Authoring custom middleware. If you are adding a whole database, @prisma/orm postgres is the one to copy for a SQL database and @prisma/orm mongo for a document database. Once your package is on npm, submit it to the directory, and a maintainer reviews your entry before it appears in the catalog. See also Using extensions install an extension and run your first query with it Supported databases which databases Prisma ORM ships and what is planned Coming from Prisma ORM 7 what changes in a project that already uses @prisma/client and schema.prisma
extensions/using-extensions: An extension is a package that teaches Prisma ORM a database feature it does not know out of the box. Installing one gives you new column types to declare and new query operations to call, along with the migrations that install the feature in the database itself. Vector search, geospatial data, full text search, typed JSON, and provider specific integrations all reach your project this way. Reach for an extension when your application needs one of those database features and you still want everything Prisma ORM gives you for the rest of your data typed schema declarations, generated TypeScript, migration support, and query helpers. Your contract is what Prisma ORM 8 calls your schema contract.prisma in place of schema.prisma . In a project made with npm create prisma@latest it is at src/prisma/contract.prisma . Adding an extension means installing its package and then registering it in two places, your config file and your client. These steps use pgvector, the vector search extension, as the example, and they assume a PostgreSQL project from Create a new app with PostgreSQL, so @prisma/orm postgres is already installed and the extension package is added next to it. Supabase is set up differently, so if that is the extension you are adding, read the note under the catalog first. 1. Install the package 2. Register it in the config A project made with npm create prisma@latest already has prisma.config.ts , so open it and add the extension to the extensions array. @prisma/orm postgres is the package you call directly ormConfig(...) in prisma.config.ts and postgres(...) in db.ts . Other extensions are listed in the extensions array passed to those two calls. The example renames defineConfig to ormConfig so it is not confused with definePrismaConfig , and you can keep the original name. Import the paths the extension's page in the extension directory gives you. For pgvector they are /control in prisma.config.ts and /runtime in db.ts . 3. Register it on the client Add the extension to the extensions array on the client as well, which is what gives the db object you write queries against the extension's query operations and value types. The './contract.d' in that import is not a typo it is how you import contract.d.ts , one of the two files npx prisma contract emit writes. 4. Use the new type in your contract [ 4 use the new type in your schema] Now that pgvector is in prisma.config.ts , npx prisma contract emit accepts pgvector.Vector(1536) in your contract. A vector column needs an explicit number of dimensions, so declare that dimension once as a named type in a types block, and then every column that uses the name gets the same dimension. The trailing ? on Embedding1536? makes the column optional, exactly as ? did in Prisma ORM 7. The types block is part of PSL syntax. The pgvector in pgvector.Vector(1536) is the name the extension registers its types under, and its page in the extension directory lists them. PostGIS, for example, gives you postgis.Geometry(4326) . The first line of the file, // use prisma 8 , is required. npx prisma contract emit reads only .prisma files whose first line is // use prisma 8 and skips any other file without a warning, so keep that line at the top when you add the types block. 5. Apply and query Getting the new column from your contract into your database takes these commands, in this order 1. npx prisma contract emit , so that contract.json and contract.d.ts pick up the new column. It also writes the extension's own files under migrations/pgvector/ its contract, its head ref and its migrations. Commit them along with your other migrations. Run it again after every later change to contract.prisma , and after you upgrade the extension package. 2. npx prisma db init on a new database, or npx prisma db update on one that already has tables, which Applying a migration covers. This runs the extension's migration and makes the database match your contract it creates the Post table, or adds the embedding column when the Post table already exists. The extension's contract declares the PostgreSQL extension vector , so its migration runs CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector and you never write that statement yourself, but the PostgreSQL server has to have pgvector available for it to succeed. Both databases the quickstart offers have it the local Prisma Postgres database that Composer starts, and a Prisma Postgres database from npx create db@latest . A stock PostgreSQL image may not, and then the migration fails on that statement, so install pgvector on the server first, following pgvector's own instructions. The extension's contract declares vector outside any schema, so db sign and db verify accept the extension in any schema on the connection's search path, such as the extensions schema Supabase installs extensions in. A Supabase database that already has pgvector, PostGIS, ParadeDB or citext there adopts Prisma ORM 8 with npx prisma contract emit and npx prisma db sign . When the extension is in a schema that is not on the search path, db verify fails and names the schema and the search path. Add that schema to the search path of the role your app connects as, or reinstall the extension in a schema on the search path. Do not declare vector in your own contract as well. contract emit refuses an extension vector {} block with PSL ENTITY DECLARED BY PACK , and migration plan and db update refuse an extension('vector') handle in a TypeScript contract. The same holds for postgis with the PostGIS extension, pg search with ParadeDB, and citext with the citext pack. note[Upgrading pgvector, PostGIS, ParadeDB or citext from before 8.0.0 rc.23 ] Since 8.0.0 rc.23 , each of these extensions declares its PostgreSQL extension outside any schema. After you upgrade, run npx prisma contract emit , which writes new migrations and a new head ref under the extension's directory in migrations/ , and commit all of them. When you upgrade from before 8.0.0 rc.22 , these include the migrations the next note describes. Then run npx prisma db migrate against each database. On a database that already ran the migrations added in 8.0.0 rc.22 , the migration it runs has no operations, so the database does not change. If your own contract declares the same extension, remove that declaration first, as described above. note[Upgrading pgvector, PostGIS or ParadeDB from before 8.0.0 rc.22 ] Since 8.0.0 rc.22 , each of these extensions declares its PostgreSQL extension in its contract, instead of installing it in a migration that records an invariant, an id the database keeps to show that migration ran. After you upgrade, run npx prisma contract emit and commit the files it writes under the extension's directory in migrations/ a new head ref and two new migrations. Then run npx prisma db migrate against each database. On a database where the old migration already installed the extension, the new migration only moves the extension's marker. On a database that has the extension but was never signed, npx prisma db sign works now. db sign refuses a contract space whose head ref needs an invariant the database has not recorded, with MIGRATION.SIGN INVARIANTS MISSING , because only db migrate can run the migration that records it. With the column in your database, write an embedding into it. A vector value is a plain number[] with as many entries as the column's dimension, so a column typed Embedding1536 takes an array of 1536 numbers, which is what an embedding model gives you. Prisma ORM does not produce the numbers, and embed in this example stands for whichever model you call In Prisma ORM 8 create takes the fields directly, with no data wrapper. Create a record shows the two side by side. public is the PostgreSQL schema your tables are in. To get the rows closest to a query vector on db.orm , use the method pgvector adds for each vector field under using . It orders the rows by cosine distance, nearest first, and an optional second argument keeps only the rows within that distance Package methods with using covers these methods. To get the distance itself in each row, write the search with the SQL query builder, as in the block below, where db.orm is the ORM API, and under it you address a model by the name in your contract, so the model Post is db.orm.public.Post . db.sql is the SQL query builder, and under it you address a table by the name it has in the database, so the same data is db.sql.public.Post . The two names are the same because the model sets no @@map . db.query(...) runs a built query. f , in the callback of each builder method, holds the row's columns. fns holds the functions you can call on those columns, including the ones pgvector adds. queryVector is a number[] of the same length as the stored embeddings. .select('distance', ...) names the computed column distance , and .build() returns a plain object that db.query(...) runs. Each row that comes back has id , title , and distance , a number that is null when the row has no embedding. Alongside fns.cosineDistance , pgvector gives you fns.cosineSimilarity . Both take two vectors and return a PostgreSQL float8 , which you get as a number . The difference is which way you sort order ascending when you sort by distance, because the closest row has the smallest distance, and descending when you sort by similarity. How the pieces fit One installed package supplies both registrations, the one in prisma.config.ts and the one in db.ts When a registration is missing [ capabilities] When your contract uses an extension and db.ts does not list it in extensions , postgres(...) throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.MISSING EXTENSION PACK before any query runs. Add the extension's runtime import to db.ts to fix it. If the database cannot install the extension, db init or db update reports it. Available extensions Every extension, whether Prisma wrote it or someone in the community did, is listed in the extension directory with its install command and the registration snippets to copy. {/ extensions catalog start not tag=middleware /} Name What it adds Package Databases By arktype json JSON columns validated by an arktype schema and typed end to end. @prisma/orm extension arktype json PostgreSQL Prisma MongoDB MongoDB support for Prisma ORM config, runtime, contract authoring, BSON values, and migrations in one package. @prisma/orm mongo MongoDB Prisma ParadeDB (experimental) BM25 full text search ranked by relevance, with fuzzy, phrase, and proximity queries. @prisma/orm extension paradedb PostgreSQL Prisma pgvector Vector columns and similarity search for embeddings. @prisma/orm extension pgvector PostgreSQL Prisma PostGIS Geometry columns and geospatial queries such as distance and containment. @prisma/orm extension postgis PostgreSQL Prisma PostgreSQL PostgreSQL support for Prisma ORM config, runtime, contract authoring, and migrations in one package. @prisma/orm postgres PostgreSQL Prisma SQLite (experimental) SQLite support for Prisma ORM config, runtime, contract authoring, and migrations in one package. @prisma/orm sqlite SQLite Prisma Supabase (experimental) Supabase auth and storage tables plus role bound clients for row level security. @prisma/orm extension supabase PostgreSQL Prisma IndexedDB (experimental) Prisma 8 for IndexedDB a browser database from your PSL schema, with typed accessors and explicit migrations. @prisma idb/client idb IndexedDB Yash Kolekar typed json Typed JSON and text columns with no validator dependency. prisma orm extension typed json PostgreSQL Omar Dulaimi zod json Typed JSON columns described and enforced by a zod schema. prisma orm extension zod json PostgreSQL Omar Dulaimi {/ extensions catalog end /} The database packages are in the table too. The ones marked experimental work today, but their methods and options are still changing between releases. Each name in the table links to that extension's directory page, and from there to the package README. Middleware wraps queries rather than adding a database feature, so it is listed on How middleware works instead. note[Supabase does not follow the recipe above] Supabase publishes no control entry point. What the command line tools read is published at @prisma/orm extension supabase/pack instead, so the config imports that and passes it to the same ormConfig(...) call step 2 uses The client is where the real difference is, because you build it with supabase() from @prisma/orm extension supabase/runtime rather than with postgres() , and it needs a way to check the JWTs your users send jwksUrl is your project's JWKS endpoint, https // .supabase.co/auth/v1/.well known/jwks.json , and it is the right option for a current Supabase project, because those sign their JWTs with ES256 keys. An older project that still signs with the shared HS256 secret passes jwtSecret instead of jwksUrl , and never both. supabase status prints a JWT SECRET even for an ES256 project, so its presence does not tell you which one yours uses. A token signed the other way is rejected with an error whose code is SUPABASE.JWT INVALID , and the message names the fix. supabase(...) takes the options postgres(...) takes, so pgvector or another extension goes in its extensions array in the same way. That includes cursor , which streams rows from a server side cursor, and binding , which takes { kind 'url', url } or { kind 'pgPool', pool } . To use a pg pool you build yourself, pass it as pg in place of url . supabase(...) takes a pg.Pool , not a pg.Client , and checks the database input when you call it. postgres(options) lists what it accepts and the error a wrong input gives. db.close() does not end a pool you pass in, so at shutdown call await db.close() and then await pool.end() . After db.close() , a query on a role bound client does not throw at the call. The promise or query result it returns rejects when you await or read it, so do that inside try / catch . You run queries through a client bound to a role, not through db itself, which has no orm or sql . db gives you three of them await db.asUser(jwt) takes the user's Supabase JWT and runs as that user. db.asAnon() runs as the anonymous role. db.asServiceRole() bypasses row level security. When a role bound client is done with a connection, it resets the connection's role before the connection goes back to the pool, so the next query on that connection does not run as that role. Each role bound client has the members a postgres(...) client uses to run queries orm , sql , raw , prepare , query , execute , toSql , enums , nativeEnums , and transaction() . The tx a role bound transaction() passes to your callback has the same members as a postgres(...) transaction, enums and nativeEnums included. For example, prepare prepares a statement you run many times with different values, as db.prepare describes. db.close() closes every role bound client and the .supabase client of db.asServiceRole() , which queries Supabase's own auth and storage tables. A query on any of them that starts after close() rejects with an error whose code is DRIVER.NOT CONNECTED ( Runtime is closed ). close() waits for queries already running, and for open role transactions, before it ends the pool it created from url . Await every role transaction before you call close() . If you add your own methods to a model by subclassing Collection , as Custom Collection subclass shows, pass the subclass to supabase(...) in the collections option, as you would to postgres(...) . The role bound clients then use it on their orm . @prisma/orm extension supabase has a contract of its own, which describes Supabase's auth and storage tables, check constraints included. Prisma read those tables from one Supabase version, supabase/postgres 17.6.1.106, and a Supabase project on another version can have a different set of check constraints. npx prisma db verify compares your database with the extension's contract as well as with yours, and when a check constraint the extension describes is missing from your database, db verify lists it and fails. You cannot fix that with a migration, because Prisma ORM never changes Supabase's own tables. Instead, open an issue on prisma/orm with the output of db verify and your Supabase version, so the extension can be updated to match. npx prisma db sign checks that a database matches your contract and then records in the database which contract it matches, and it records the extension's contract the same way. When an update to @prisma/orm extension supabase changes the extension's contract, that record no longer matches, and npx prisma db verify fails with MIGRATION.CONTRACT SPACE VIOLATION until you run npx prisma db sign again against every database you signed with the earlier version. The Prisma ORM release notes say when an update changes the extension's contract, for example for the change introduced in 8.0.0 rc.12. A change introduced in 8.0.0 rc.20 changed it again, so after you upgrade from a version before 8.0.0 rc.20 , run npx prisma db sign against every Supabase database. The database itself does not change. If you are also re emitting your own contract with npx prisma contract emit , run that before db sign . If the extension you need does not exist yet, you can build it. An extension is an npm package with a documented layout, and the call for extension authors explains how to write and publish one. Once yours is on npm, submit it to the directory, where the form validates your entry and opens the pull request for you. See also Advanced queries the SQL query builder, where extension operations like cosineDistance appear How middleware works for wrapping queries rather than adding database features Create a new app with PostgreSQL to set up a project to add extensions to Extensions overview for the full catalog, including middleware Prisma ORM overview for how your contract, your migrations, and your client fit together
extensions/postgis: The PostGIS extension adds a geometry column to Prisma ORM 8 a point, a line, or a polygon stored in PostgreSQL by PostGIS. You write and read the values as GeoJSON shaped objects, and you query them with conditions such as "within 5 km of this point" or "inside this area". This page assumes a Prisma ORM 8 project on PostgreSQL, such as one from Create a new app with PostgreSQL src/prisma/contract.prisma is your contract, the Prisma ORM 8 name for the schema file, and src/prisma/db.ts creates the client your code queries with. PostGIS has to be installable on your PostgreSQL server. Most managed providers include it. To run it on your machine, use the postgis/postgis Docker image A database on your machine shows the Compose file, and you change its image to postgis/postgis 17 3.5 . Set it up Install the package next to @prisma/orm postgres A Prisma ORM 8 extension is a package that both the prisma command line tool and your app's client load, not a Prisma ORM 7 client extension made with $extends . Add it in two files in prisma.config.ts , import it from /control and add it to extensions ; in src/prisma/db.ts , import it from /runtime and add it to extensions . Keep the rest of each file as it is; the full files look like this Declare a geometry column A geometry column stores shapes in one coordinate system, named by a number called the SRID. SRID 4326 is longitude and latitude in degrees, the system GPS and most maps use. postgis.Geometry(4326) is a column in that system; name it once in a types block and use the name on each field The column can hold any shape a point, a line, or a polygon. The gist index is the kind PostGIS searches shapes with; without one, PostgreSQL checks every row. In a TypeScript contract, the column is field.column(type.postgis.Geometry(4326)) , and the contract also passes the extension's /pack to defineContract as { extensions { postgis } } , as TypeScript schema builder shows for pgvector. Then update the generated files, write the migration, and apply it to your development database migration plan writes your migration under migrations/app/ , and contract emit has already written the extension's files under migrations/postgis/ , whose migration installs PostGIS in the database. Commit both. PostGIS may already be installed in another schema on the connection's search path, such as the extensions schema on Supabase, and db sign and db verify accept it there. Do not declare extension postgis {} in your own contract, because the extension declares it. Generating a migration explains advance ref db . Write and read shapes A geometry value is a GeoJSON shaped object. The package's /geojson entry point has functions that build one point(longitude, latitude) , polygon(ring) , and bboxPolygon([minLongitude, minLatitude, maxLongitude, maxLatitude]) . Longitude comes first, as in GeoJSON. Each function takes the SRID as its last argument. When you write a shape without one, it takes the column's, and a read returns the shape in the form the comment shows. When you write a shape with a different SRID, PostgreSQL refuses it with Geometry SRID (3857) does not match column SRID (4326) . In a query, always pass the SRID a shape you compare the column with has no SRID unless you give one, and then every operation below except distanceSphere and intersectsBbox fails with Operation on mixed SRID geometries . Find rows by distance or area Each geometry field has these operations, which you use in where() Operation Is true, or returns location.distanceSphere(other) the distance in meters, measured on the earth's surface location.distance(other) the distance in the column's units, which are degrees for 4326 location.dwithin(other, distance) true when the two are within distance , in the column's units location.within(area) true when the shape is inside area location.contains(other) true when the shape contains other location.intersects(other) true when the two shapes touch or overlap location.intersectsBbox(other) true when the rectangles around the two shapes overlap, which is a faster, rougher test than intersects For "within 5 km" on a 4326 column, compare distanceSphere with a number of meters, using lt , lte , gt , or gte . distanceSphere cannot use the gist index, so PostgreSQL checks every row; put dwithin with a radius in degrees in front of it, which uses the index to narrow the rows first. A tenth of a degree is more than 5 km in every direction between 60 degrees south and 60 degrees north dwithin subtracts longitudes without wrapping at 180 degrees, so this query misses a place on the other side of the line where longitude jumps from 180 to 180 179.99 and 179.99 are 2 km apart at the equator but 359.98 degrees apart for dwithin . Closer to the poles than 60 degrees, 5 km east or west is more than a tenth of a degree, so use a larger radius there. To find the places inside an area, pass a polygon. A ring is the list of [longitude, latitude] corners, and polygon() closes it for you To return the distance with each row and sort by it, write the query with the SQL query builder. There, you address the table by its name in the database, which is the model's name unless the model sets @@map . f holds the table's columns, and fns holds the same operations, which take the column as their first argument Next steps Using extensions walks through the same setup for pgvector, step by step. PostGIS's own documentation covers coordinate systems and which queries use an index.
extensions/paradedb: The ParadeDB extension adds full text search to Prisma ORM 8, with results ranked by how well they match. It uses pg search , a PostgreSQL extension from ParadeDB. pg search adds a BM25 index, which ranks results the way most search engines do. You declare one index over the text columns to search, and then filter and rank rows by a search query. @prisma/orm extension paradedb is experimental what it offers may change in a later Prisma ORM release, so check its release notes before you upgrade. This page assumes a Prisma ORM 8 project on PostgreSQL, such as one from Create a new app with PostgreSQL, where src/prisma/db.ts creates the client your code queries with. pg search has to be installed on your PostgreSQL server. Check that your provider offers it; ParadeDB's documentation lists where it runs. To run it on your machine, use the paradedb/paradedb Docker image A database on your machine shows the Compose file, and you change its image to paradedb/paradedb . Your contract must be TypeScript The search index can only be declared in a TypeScript contract, src/prisma/contract.ts ; a contract.prisma contract cannot declare it yet. A project has one contract, so if yours is contract.prisma , rewrite it in TypeScript and delete contract.prisma TypeScript schema builder shows the TypeScript form of everything you can write in contract.prisma . Then change contract in prisma.config.ts to ./src/prisma/contract.ts . When the rewrite describes the same tables, migration plan finds nothing to change. Set it up Install the package next to @prisma/orm postgres A Prisma ORM 8 extension is a package that both the prisma command line tool and your app's client load, not a Prisma ORM 7 client extension made with $extends . Add it in three places in prisma.config.ts from /control , in src/prisma/db.ts from /runtime , and in the contract from /pack , the part defineContract uses. Keep the rest of each file as it is; the full files look like this Declare the search index In the contract, pass the pack to defineContract with the key paradedb , and add the index with constraints.index List the key column and every column you want to search. key field names the column that identifies each row, usually the primary key. The package requires it, although pg search 0.26 and newer ignore it. The table is named after the model, Article , as it would be from contract.prisma . Then update the generated files, write the migration, and apply it to your development database migration plan writes your migration under migrations/app/ , and contract emit has already written the extension's files under migrations/paradedb/ , whose migration installs pg search in the database. Commit both. pg search may already be installed in another schema on the connection's search path, and db sign and db verify accept it there. Do not declare extension pg search {} in your own contract, because the extension declares it. Generating a migration explains advance ref db . Search Each text column in the index has search operations, which you use in where() . A search splits the column's text and your query into words, ignoring case Operation Matches rows whose field body.paradeDbMatch(query) or body.paradeDbMatchAny(query) contains any word of query body.paradeDbMatchAll(query) contains every word of query body.paradeDbPhrase(query) contains the words of query next to each other, in order body.paradeDbTerm(word) contains the one word word , compared as written, so give it in lowercase To search the title and the body with one query, combine two matches with or To rank results, write the query with the SQL query builder. There, f holds the table's columns, and fns holds the same operations, which take the column as their first argument. paradeDbScore takes the key column and returns each row's relevance, higher for a better match. It needs a ParadeDB filter in the same query, as this one has; without one, PostgreSQL refuses the query with pdb.score must be evaluated by a ParadeDB scan Next steps Using extensions walks through the setup for pgvector, step by step. ParadeDB's own documentation covers how text is split into words and its query syntax.
extensions/arktype-json: A plain Jsonb column, Prisma ORM 8's type for a PostgreSQL jsonb column, reads as any JSON value, so your code has to check what is in it. The arktype json extension describes a JSON column with an arktype schema instead. The column's TypeScript type then comes from the schema, and Prisma ORM checks each value against the schema when it reads it. The column is still a jsonb column, so it needs nothing installed on the server. This page assumes a Prisma ORM 8 project on PostgreSQL, such as one from Create a new app with PostgreSQL, where src/prisma/db.ts creates the client your code queries with. Your contract must be TypeScript The schema is a JavaScript value, so the column is declared in a TypeScript contract, src/prisma/contract.ts ; a contract.prisma contract cannot hold it. A project has one contract, so if yours is contract.prisma , rewrite it in TypeScript first TypeScript schema builder shows the TypeScript form of each PSL construct. Then set contract in prisma.config.ts to ./src/prisma/contract.ts . Set it up Install the package and arktype next to @prisma/orm postgres A Prisma ORM 8 extension is a package that both the prisma command line tool and your app's client load, not a Prisma ORM 7 client extension made with $extends . Add it in three places in prisma.config.ts from /control , in src/prisma/db.ts from /runtime , and in the contract from /pack , the part defineContract uses. Keep the rest of each file as it is; the full files look like this Declare the column In the contract, pass the pack to defineContract with the key "arktype json" , in quotes because of the hyphen; with any other key, the client fails to start with RUNTIME.MISSING EXTENSION PACK . Then make the column with arktypeJson(schema) from /column types The builder's own type helper is renamed to t here, because arktype's type has the same name. ArticleMeta is exported so your app can check values with it too. .optional() lets the column be empty, which reads as null . Then update the generated files, write the migration, and apply it to your development database Two changes leave the database as it is, because the column stays jsonb switching an existing Jsonb column to arktypeJson(...) , and changing the arktype type later. After either one, run npx prisma contract emit so the column's TypeScript type follows. migration plan then stops with MIGRATION.PLANNING FAILED and prints a command 1. Run the printed npx prisma migration new from . It writes a migration with no operations, which records the new contract. 2. Run npx prisma db migrate advance ref db . Rows already in the column are not checked until they are read. Read and write the column contract emit writes the schema's TypeScript type into contract.d.ts , so meta reads as { tags string[]; readingMinutes? number } , and TypeScript checks what you write Prisma ORM checks a value against the schema when it reads it, not when it writes it. A row whose stored value breaks the schema, written by SQL or by another app, fails to read with an error whose code is RUNTIME.JSON SCHEMA VALIDATION FAILED , and the message names the problem, such as tags must be an array (was number) . In a query that returns many rows, one such row fails the whole query. Because writes are not checked, a value typed any or unknown , such as a parsed request body, reaches the database unchecked. What happens next depends on the method create() saves the row, then throws RUNTIME.JSON SCHEMA VALIDATION FAILED when it reads the row back. The row stays in the database. update() throws the same error and does not save the change. createAndCount() and updateAndCount() do not read rows back, so they save the value and throw nothing. Check such a value with the arktype type before you write it To repair a row that fails to read, overwrite its value update() does not read the old value, so db.orm.public.Article.where({ id }).update({ meta { tags [] } }) works on it. Find such rows with SQL, such as SELECT id FROM article WHERE meta IS NOT NULL AND jsonb typeof(meta 'tags') IS DISTINCT FROM 'array' , which also finds values with no tags key; the table is article because the contract sets table 'article' . Next steps Using extensions walks through the setup for pgvector, step by step. arktype's own documentation covers how to write a schema.
reference: Prisma ORM gives you three typed ways to write a query. In Prisma ORM 7 you wrote findMany({ where, include }) , but now each of those arguments is a method you chain .where(...).include(...) . See Coming from Prisma ORM 7, which maps each argument to its method. The ORM client is at db.orm . It has model methods such as where() , create() , and include() , it works on both PostgreSQL and MongoDB, and it covers everyday reads and writes across your models. The SQL query builder is at db.sql . It has table methods that match SQL, such as select() , innerJoin() , and groupBy() , it is PostgreSQL only, and it returns whatever shape your select() asks for, not objects shaped like your models. The pipeline builder is at db.query . It builds MongoDB aggregation pipelines, and it is MongoDB only. When none of the three can express the query you need, write raw SQL on PostgreSQL or a raw command on MongoDB. See Raw queries. For connecting and disconnecting the client, transactions, and prepared statements, see Transactions and runtime. Running a query The ORM client sends its own queries first() , create() , update() , upsert() , delete() , and aggregate() send the query the moment you call them. all() , createAll() , updateAll() , and deleteAll() return a result object and send the query when you await that object or loop over it with for await . all() is what replaced findMany . The SQL query builder and the pipeline builder send nothing on their own .build() gives you a built query. Pass it to runtime.query(...) for rows, or to runtime.execute(...) for a write that returns no rows. Get runtime from db.runtime() once and reuse it. PostgreSQL User is the model name and user is the table name, which the example schema sets with @@map("user") . Without @@map , the two names are the same. The ORM client compares on the column, u.kind.eq(...) , while the SQL query builder compares through fns , fns.eq(f.kind, ...) . MongoDB db.runtime() returns a promise on MongoDB, so await it. users is the collection name, and both db.orm and db.query.from() are keyed by it. The ORM client's where() takes an object of field values, while the pipeline builder's match() takes a callback that compares on the field, f.role.eq(...) . Two different things are named query db.query builds a pipeline, and runtime.query(...) runs a query that has already been built. } Every ORM client method, with PostgreSQL and MongoDB behavior documented side by side. } Every SQL query builder method for building typed, table level queries against PostgreSQL. } Every MongoDB pipeline builder stage, accumulator, expression helper, and write method. } Raw SQL on PostgreSQL and raw commands on MongoDB, for queries the typed APIs cannot express. } Connecting and disconnecting the client, transactions, prepared statements, and execution options. } Every method and helper a migration.ts can call, with the SQL each PostgreSQL operation runs, and the MongoDB operations.
reference/orm-client: The ORM client gives you model level methods for reading and writing data across PostgreSQL and MongoDB. This page documents every method, its availability on each database, and the behavior that differs between the two. Each method's Remarks say which databases it works on, how it behaves differently on one of them, and where TypeScript rejects something the database itself would accept. This page assumes your tables already exist. Coming from Prisma ORM 7 has the packages to install and the prisma orm init command. It also covers prisma db update , which replaces prisma migrate dev , and prisma contract emit , which replaces prisma generate . How migrations work shows how the tables get created. For task oriented walkthroughs, see the Fundamentals guides Reading data, Writing data, Relations and joins, and Transactions. Example schema All examples on this page run against the schema below, except the grouped aggregate ones, which use a separate Customer / Order schema shown under Grouped aggregates, and the row locking example, which uses a Job model shown beside it. contract.prisma replaces schema.prisma , and this page calls it the contract. Running npx prisma contract emit compiles it into two generated files contract.json , read at run time, and contract.d.ts , read by TypeScript. You import both, as the examples below do. Run npx prisma contract emit again after every change to contract.prisma . A new project keeps all three files in src/prisma/ . Expand for the example schema Some parts of the schema the examples rely on The types block at the top gives a name to a type from an extension package, so your models can use that name. Embedding1536 comes from the pgvector extension, and pgvector. is that package's prefix. See PostgreSQL for the extra line it needs when you create the client. @@map("user") sets the table or collection name. Without it, the table name is the model name exactly as written, User . On MongoDB, id ObjectId @id @map(" id") stores the field as id in the database. The ORM names it id , its name in the schema you filter on id , write id , and the returned document has an id key. The same holds for every field with @map . The pipeline builder and raw commands work on stored documents, so they name the field id . Uuid is a built in type for a PostgreSQL uuid column. You do not import it. @onCreate(uuid()) makes Prisma ORM fill the id in when you insert a row. @@type("pg/text@1") on an enum block stores the enum as a text column. The @1 is the version of that storage format, and only version 1 exists today, so write it exactly like that. The MongoDB form of the same attribute is @@type("mongo/string@1") . This page calls an enum written this way a text backed enum. A native enum block stores the members as a PostgreSQL enum type, created with CREATE TYPE . Prisma ORM 7 stored every enum this way, so a database that Prisma ORM 7 created already has these types, and you keep them by declaring each one with native enum , as Coming from Prisma ORM 7 shows. A plain enum block in Prisma ORM 8 is stored as text. Give every native enum member a value, because a member with no value is rejected. A field that uses it is typed pg.enum(Priority) . This page calls an enum written this way a native enum. The two sort differently; see orderBy() . prisma native enum Priority { Low = "low" High = "high" Urgent = "urgent" } model Post { id Uuid @id @onCreate(uuid()) priority pg.enum(Priority) } An enum member's stored value is the string after = , or the member name when there is no = . That string is what you pass to .eq() . So Urgent = "urgent" is matched by .eq('urgent') , and a bare admin member is matched by .eq('admin') . A variant is a model that reuses another model's fields and rows. @@base(Task, "bug") makes Bug a variant of Task . Its second argument, "bug" , is the value stored in the discriminator column for a Bug row. @@discriminator(type) names that column. db.orm.public.Task.variant('bug') returns only the Bug rows. Pass the string in @@base , 'bug' , not the model name. PostTag is required. To join Post.tags Tag[] and Tag.posts Post[] , write a third model with one foreign key to each side and an @@id of exactly those two columns. Prisma ORM finds it for you, and neither Post nor Tag names it. A pair of list fields with no such model is rejected. See Relations and joins. On PostgreSQL, a DateTime field comes back as a JavaScript Date , and a field written DateTime(as temporal) as a Temporal.Instant . A filter on a field takes the same type it returns, so you can pass a value straight back in. Setting up the client Create a client with postgres(...) or mongo(...) , then read and write your models through db.orm . The same db also has a query builder, db.sql on PostgreSQL and db.query on MongoDB, plus db.raw for raw queries. This page covers none of those three see Advanced queries. Create db once per process, and close it with await db.close() when the process shuts down. The two databases have different entry points, and they name the models differently. PostgreSQL Create a PostgreSQL client with postgres(...) . db.orm holds your models by model name, grouped by database schema db.orm.public.User , db.orm.public.Post . public is the PostgreSQL schema your tables are in unless you put them in another one. Import types from ./contract.d , which resolves to contract.d.ts . If your contract uses a type from an extension package, pass that package to extensions when you create the client. The example schema's Embedding1536 type comes from pgvector, so it needs this To give a model your own methods on top of the built in ones, import Collection from @prisma/orm postgres/orm client , subclass it, and pass the subclass to postgres(...) in the collections option. The code is under Custom Collection subclass. MongoDB Create a MongoDB client with mongo(...) . db.orm holds your models by collection name, with no schema in between. The collection name is the one you set with @@map , or the model name exactly as written when you did not set one. The example schema maps User to users , so it is db.orm.users , and Post is db.orm.posts . dbName is the MongoDB database name. Query building methods These methods narrow a query, and each returns a collection. On this page, a collection is the query object you chain more methods on, such as db.orm.public.User or db.orm.public.User.where(...) . When this page says "a MongoDB collection", it means that query object. MongoDB itself calls its store of documents a collection too, and the name is the same one. You run the query with a read method such as all() or first() . MongoDB supports fewer of these methods than PostgreSQL, and each method's Remarks say which databases it works on. Some examples import a filter helper you can use on its own. On PostgreSQL those come from @prisma/orm postgres/orm client , on MongoDB from @prisma/orm mongo/query ast/execution . See Filter conditions and operators. The examples below use these ids, which stand for rows inserted before the query runs where() Restrict a query to rows matching a filter. Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB, but the accepted filter shapes differ. On PostgreSQL, where() takes either a callback that calls an operator on a column ( u.email.eq(...) ) or an object of field and value pairs that must match exactly. On MongoDB, where() takes either an object of field and value pairs that must match exactly or a MongoFieldFilter . The object form can only test for equality. For anything else, such as greater than, use MongoFieldFilter (see MongoFieldFilter). Calling where() more than once on the same query requires a row to match all of the filters. A filter value has the type you write to the field. A field whose type has parameters, such as String(storage varchar, length 50) , reads as Varchar but takes a plain string in where() , first() , create() , update() , and upsert() , so you need no cast. The same holds for Char and Numeric . .eq() is one operator of many. Filter conditions and operators, further down this page, lists them all for both databases. Options Argument Type Required Description filter A callback that calls an operator on a column, a shorthand object, or (MongoDB) a MongoFieldFilter Yes The condition rows must satisfy. Return type Return type Example Description Collection db.orm.public.User.where(...) A collection narrowed by the filter. Chain more methods on it, then run it with a read or write method. Examples Callback form with a column operator (PostgreSQL) Shorthand object form Chaining where() calls (ANDed) MongoFieldFilter expression (MongoDB) For a task oriented guide to filtering, see Reading data. whereUnique() Restrict a query to the one row a primary key or a unique constraint names. Remarks PostgreSQL only. The criterion is an object with a value for every field of the primary key or of one @@unique constraint, such as { id } , { email } or { tenantId, userId } . A field that is not part of such a key, or a key with a field missing, is a type error. When the call runs, a criterion without a value for every field of one key throws an error whose code is ORM.ARGUMENT INVALID . It filters exactly as where() with the same object does. A value cannot be null , because a unique constraint allows any number of rows whose column is NULL ; to read those, use where({ field null }) . After it, the calls that address many rows are compile errors orderBy() , limit() , offset() , cursor() , distinct() , distinctOn() , all() , aggregate() , groupBy() , updateAll() , updateAndCount() , deleteAll() , deleteAndCount() , and prepared.all() and prepared.aggregate() . first() , firstOrThrow() , update() , delete() , select() , include() and a further where() still compile. Inside an include() refinement it throws an error whose code is ORM.INCLUDE INVALID . Examples select() Return only the scalar fields you name. Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB. On PostgreSQL, select() narrows the returned row shape at the type level fields you didn't select are absent from the result type. On MongoDB, select() changes what the database returns but not the TypeScript type. Only the fields you named come back. The type still lists every field on the model. Read a field you did not name and you get undefined , because the returned document does not carry it. Options Argument Type Required Description ...fields Field names ( string ) Yes One or more scalar field names to keep. Return type Return type Example Description Collection db.orm.public.User.select('id', 'email') A collection projected to the named fields. Examples Project to a subset of fields include() Eagerly load a relation onto the returned rows. Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB, with differences noted below. On PostgreSQL, include(relationName, refineFn?) loads both to one and to many relations. The optional callback receives the related rows as a collection, so you can filter, order, limit, and aggregate them. See Refinements, aggregates, and combine. On MongoDB, wrap the id of a related document loaded by include() in String(...) before you compare it. It comes back as an ObjectId object, while a document's own id comes back as a hex string. On MongoDB, include() loads a relation that is stored as a reference. It takes the relation name and nothing else, and TypeScript rejects a second argument. Options Argument Type Required Description relationName string Yes The relation to load. refineFn A callback that returns the narrowed relation or an aggregate of it No PostgreSQL only. Narrows the loaded relation, or reduces it to one value. Return type Return type Example Description Collection db.orm.public.User.include('posts') A collection whose rows carry the loaded relation. Examples To one relation (PostgreSQL) To many relation (PostgreSQL) Reference relation (MongoDB) For a task oriented guide to loading related records, see Relations and joins. Refinements, aggregates, and combine On PostgreSQL, the callback you pass to include() receives the related rows as a collection. This page calls that callback a refinement, which is the word in the heading above. You can filter, order, and paginate the related rows in it, and you can also reduce them to a single value, or use combine() to return several results at once. To count or sum a whole model instead of a relation, see Grouped aggregates, where aggregate((agg) = ({ n agg.count() })) counts every row. Remarks PostgreSQL only. On MongoDB, include() takes no callback, and count , sum , avg , min , max , and combine do not exist on a collection. On PostgreSQL, those six are only callable inside an include() callback. Called anywhere else, they throw an error whose code is ORM.INCLUDE INVALID . sum() and avg() take a numeric column an integer, a floating point number, or a decimal. They also take an interval or a Time column, the time of day type. They do not take a date or a timestamp, and TypeScript rejects a date or timestamp field name here. min() and max() take more numeric and text columns, dates, times, timestamps, intervals, IP addresses, and text arrays. They do not take a boolean, a uuid , binary data, a bit string, or JSON. count() returns a number . With no argument it counts rows; with a field name it counts rows where that field is not null. countBigInt() returns a bigint instead, for a count too large for a JavaScript number . sum() over an integer column returns a number . A total too large for a number throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.DECODE FAILED . Use sumBigInt(field) for totals that large. It returns a bigint . avg() over an integer column returns a JavaScript floating point number . avgDecimal(field) returns the exact average as a decimal string. Pass that string to a decimal library, or call Number(...) on it when a floating point value is fine. When a to many relation has no rows, sum() , avg() , min() , and max() come back as null , not 0 . combine(shape) takes an object. You choose the keys. Call posts.combine({ ... }) , and inside the object write posts again for each value. The posts inside the object is the same collection the callback received, with nothing chained on it yet. A value that chains more methods on posts comes back as an array of rows. A value that is an aggregate, such as posts.count() , comes back as that single value. Options Argument Type Required Description where() / orderBy() / limit() / offset() Chained on the nested collection No Refine which related rows load. count() Aggregate, no arguments No Reduces the relation to a row count. sum(field) / avg(field) Aggregate over a numeric field No Reduces the relation to one number. min(field) / max(field) Aggregate over a sortable field No Reduces the relation to its smallest or largest value, in the column's own type. combine(shape) Object of named collections and aggregates No Returns several results under one relation key. Return type Return type Example Description The narrowed relation, a single value, or an object of both include('posts', (p) = p.count()) The relation key on each row holds the callback's result instead of the related rows. Examples Filter, order, and limit within a relation (PostgreSQL) Reduce a relation to a count (PostgreSQL) sum() / avg() over a numeric relation (PostgreSQL) This example uses the Customer and Order models, which are in the separate schema shown under Grouped aggregates. combine() multiple sub views (PostgreSQL) note[ min() and max() over a date column] min('createdAt') over a DateTime column compiles and returns the field's type, a JavaScript Date . Over a field read as a Temporal value, it returns that value, which needs a global Temporal check with typeof Temporal === 'undefined' , and if your engine has none, install temporal polyfill and add import 'temporal polyfill/full/global' . sum('createdAt') and avg('createdAt') do not compile. orderBy() Sort the result set. Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB, with different argument shapes. On PostgreSQL, orderBy() takes a callback that returns .asc() or .desc() on one column. Pass an array of such callbacks to sort by more than one column. On PostgreSQL, the callback can also sort by a field of a related record, for a relation to one record and one relation deep, as in (p) = p.user.displayName.asc() . On PostgreSQL, the callback can also sort by the number of related records, for a relation to many records, as in (u) = u.posts.count().desc() . count() takes an optional filter, the same one some() takes. On PostgreSQL, .asc() and .desc() take { nulls "first" } or { nulls "last" } . Without it, PostgreSQL puts nulls last for .asc() and first for .desc() . On MongoDB, orderBy() takes an object instead { field 1 } sorts ascending and { field 1 } sorts descending. The example schema declares Priority text backed, so on PostgreSQL it sorts by its stored text 'high' , then 'low' , then 'urgent' . A native enum column sorts in the order its members are declared instead, so the same members in a native enum Priority block sort Low , High , Urgent . Use a native enum when the sort order matters. Options Argument Type Required Description sort Callback (fields) = f.field.asc() \ .desc() , an array of such callbacks (PostgreSQL), or a { field 1 \ 1 } object (MongoDB) Yes The sort key(s) and direction(s). Return type Return type Example Description Collection db.orm.public.Post.orderBy(...) A collection with an ordering applied. Examples Ascending and descending Multiple sort keys (PostgreSQL) limit() Limit the number of returned rows. Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB. Options Argument Type Required Description count number Yes Maximum number of rows to return. Return type Return type Example Description Collection db.orm.public.Post.limit(2) A collection limited to count rows. Examples Limit the result set offset() Offset into the ordered result set. Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB. Combine with orderBy() and limit() for pagination. Options Argument Type Required Description count number Yes Number of rows to skip. Return type Return type Example Description Collection db.orm.public.Post.offset(2) A collection offset by count rows. Examples Offset into the result set Related records, counts, and nulls (PostgreSQL) cursor() Resume pagination from a known position. Remarks PostgreSQL only. cursor() does not exist on a MongoDB collection. Every sort in the orderBy() must be a plain column of the model. A sort by a related record, a count, an extension operation such as a vector distance, or a sort with nulls makes cursor() throw an error whose code is ORM.ARGUMENT INVALID . Page such a query with limit() and offset() . Always call orderBy() before cursor() . TypeScript rejects the call if you do not. Nothing checks this while the query runs, so without the orderBy() the cursor is ignored and every row comes back. The cursor object must name every column the orderBy() sorts on. Leave one out and running the query throws an error whose code is ORM.CURSOR VALUE MISSING . With two sort columns, give both keys. The cursor compares the sort columns in order first by the first column, then by the second for rows that tie on the first. Options Argument Type Required Description values Object of the orderBy() key(s) and their values Yes The position to resume after. Return type Return type Example Description Collection db.orm.public.Post.cursor({ createdAt }) A collection resuming after the cursor position. Examples Resume pagination (PostgreSQL) distinct() Remove duplicate rows, comparing only the fields you name. Remarks PostgreSQL only. distinct() does not exist on a MongoDB collection. You do not need select() . distinct('priority') keeps one whole row per distinct priority value, whatever the query returns. Which of the tied rows it keeps is not defined. Call orderBy() first to choose, as distinctOn() does. Options Argument Type Required Description ...fields Field names ( string ) Yes The fields to deduplicate on. Return type Return type Example Description Collection db.orm.public.Post.distinct('priority') A collection with duplicate rows removed on the named fields. Examples Deduplicate on a field (PostgreSQL) distinctOn() Keep the first row per key according to orderBy() . Remarks PostgreSQL only. distinctOn() does not exist on a MongoDB collection. Call orderBy() first, so that "the first row per key" means something. TypeScript rejects the call if you do not. Start the orderBy() with the same columns you pass to distinctOn() , as the example does. Sort by anything else first and the query fails in the database. If one of those first sorts is not a plain column, the call throws an error whose code is ORM.ARGUMENT INVALID ; a sort by a related record or a count may follow them. Options Argument Type Required Description ...fields Field names ( string ) Yes The key field(s) to keep the first row of. Return type Return type Example Description Collection db.orm.public.Post.distinctOn('userId') A collection keeping one row per key. Examples First row per key (PostgreSQL) variant() Narrow a model to one of the variants declared with @@base . Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB. Pass the variant's discriminator value, the string in its @@base attribute, such as 'bug' for @@base(Task, "bug") , not its model name. A value the model does not declare, or a call on a model with no @@discriminator , throws ORM.ARGUMENT INVALID . Call variant() once, on the base model. A second variant() call on a narrowed collection throws select each variant from the base model instead. On PostgreSQL, a variant that sets its own @@map , as Bug and Feature do, is stored in its own table. Read createAndCount() and upsert() before you write to such a variant. On MongoDB, every variant is a document in the one collection, told apart by the field named in @@discriminator . Options Argument Type Required Description value string Yes The discriminator value the variant declares in @@base . Return type Return type Example Description Collection , narrowed to the variant db.orm.public.Task.variant('bug') A collection holding only rows of that variant. Examples Narrow to a variant Row locking forUpdate() , forNoKeyUpdate() , forShare() , forKeyShare() [ row locking] Lock the rows a read selects until the transaction ends. Remarks PostgreSQL only. Each method exists only when the contract records that your packages support it, under these keys sql.forUpdate , postgres.forNoKeyUpdate , sql.forShare , or postgres.forKeyShare , and also sql.lockOf , because the ORM always locks only the model's own table ( FOR UPDATE OF "job" ). A contract emitted before 8.0.0 rc.17 has none of them run prisma contract emit again to get them. See what your packages support. A lock lasts until the transaction ends, so call these methods on tx.orm inside db.transaction(...) . A lock cannot be combined with include() , groupBy() , aggregate() , distinct() , distinctOn() , or a write method, and cannot be called inside an include() refinement. Each of these throws ORM.LOCK INCOMPATIBLE . Options Argument Type Required Description nowait boolean No Fail at once when another transaction holds a lock on a selected row. Needs the sql.lockNowait key in the contract. skipLocked boolean No Leave out rows another transaction has locked. Needs the sql.lockSkipLocked key in the contract. Cannot be combined with nowait . Return type Return type Example Description Collection tx.orm.public.Job.where({ state 'queued' }).forUpdate() The same collection, which locks the rows it reads. Examples Take the next queued job (PostgreSQL) This example uses a Job model Read methods [ read terminals] A read method runs the query and gives you the rows. all() and first() are available on both databases, while aggregate() and groupBy() are PostgreSQL only and are documented under Grouped aggregates. There is no count() method on either database, so on PostgreSQL, count with aggregate((a) = ({ n a.count() })) . On MongoDB, counting takes two steps db.query , the pipeline builder, builds the pipeline, and runtime.query(...) runs it. For a task oriented walkthrough, see Reading data. all() Resolve the query to every matching row. Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB. all() returns an AsyncIterableResult you can await it to collect an array, or use for await to stream rows one at a time. await ing a result you have already await ed is safe. You get the same array back, and the query does not run again. Each result can be used one way only, so awaiting it and then looping it with for await , or the reverse, throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.ITERATOR CONSUMED . See Single consumption and mode switching. orderBy() is written differently on each database. See orderBy() . Options all() takes no required arguments. Return type Return type Example Description AsyncIterableResult await db.orm.public.User.all() Awaitable to Row[] , or iterable with for await for streaming. Row is the model's row type, from the emitted contract.d.ts . Examples Await to collect an array Stream rows one at a time For Prisma ORM 7 users, findMany maps onto all() first() Resolve the query to the first matching row, or null if none matches. Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB. On PostgreSQL, first() accepts an inline filter a shorthand object or a callback ( first((p) = p.priority.eq('urgent')) ). An inline filter is added to any earlier where() call, and both have to match. On MongoDB, first() takes no filter argument. Filter with where(...) first, then call first() . Options Name Type Required Description filter Shorthand object or callback (PostgreSQL only) No An inline filter applied before resolving. Return type Return type Example Description Row \ null await db.orm.public.User.first(...) The first matching row, or null . Examples Match by an inline filter (PostgreSQL) Match with a prior where() (MongoDB) For Prisma ORM 7 users, findUnique and findFirst map onto first() , and their OrThrow forms onto firstOrThrow() first() returns null on no match and does not check that only one row matched. whereUnique() checks at compile time that the criterion names one row. firstOrThrow() Resolve the query to the first matching row, or throw when none matches. Remarks Available for PostgreSQL and MongoDB. It runs the query first() runs, with LIMIT 1 , and returns the row type without null . When nothing matches, it throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.NO ROWS . On PostgreSQL it takes the same inline filter as first() , and .prepared.firstOrThrow() is its prepared form. On MongoDB it takes no argument. The result of all() also has a firstOrThrow() method. That one reads every matching row into memory first, so prefer the collection method. Examples Custom Collection subclass On PostgreSQL and SQLite you can subclass Collection to add your own methods to a model, and pass the subclass to the client in the collections option. Remarks PostgreSQL and SQLite. You cannot subclass a collection on MongoDB. collections maps a model name to your class. You pass it to the function that creates your client postgres(...) , postgresServerless(...) for serverless functions, sqlite(...) for SQLite, or supabase(...) for Supabase. Your class is then used wherever that client gives you the model on db.orm , on every transaction's tx.orm , on each connection the serverless client opens, and on the Supabase clients that run queries as a database role, such as the one asUser(jwt) returns. Models you leave out keep the built in class. If the module that defines your classes needs the contract type, import only the type, import type { Contract } from './contract.d' , so that it does not import the module that creates the client. Collection takes two type arguments your contract type, and the name of the model this collection is for. A method that returns this.variant('bug') gives back a collection narrowed to the Bug model. It is chainable, so you finish it with all() , first() , or any other method. Your methods stay available after where() , orderBy() , limit() , offset() , include() , distinct() , distinctOn() , and cursor() , because each of them returns the collection's own class. db.orm.public.Task.where({ title }).bugs() compiles. To override one of those chaining methods, or a method that returns rows, give the override a type parameter for the receiver and a this parameter of that type, and call the base method with call override limit (this Self, n number) Self { return super.limit.call (this, Math.min(n, 100)); } . with , fragment , and using are members of every collection. A member of your own named with or fragment with another signature does not compile, and neither does a member of your own named using . See Query fragments and Package methods with using . The type PostgresClient describes a client without classes, and a client with classes fits it too. To name a client with classes, pass them as the second type argument PostgresClient . Examples Register a subclass with a domain method (PostgreSQL) The last line runs inside a transaction, so your method works on tx.orm too. forUpdate() locks the rows it reads with FOR UPDATE until the transaction ends. On SQLite, db.orm holds the models directly, so the same method is db.orm.Task.bugs() . Package methods with using [ package methods with using] Packages add methods to a model's collection under its using member. Which methods a model has depends on its fields and indexes. Remarks PostgreSQL. Each method returns a collection, so you chain it with where() , orderBy() , limit() , and the other methods, and finish with all() or first() . @prisma/orm postgres adds one method for each full text index, named after the index. It takes a search query, the same kind that fullTextMatches() takes, keeps the rows that match it, and orders them by relevance, best match first. @prisma/orm extension pgvector adds one method for each vector fi
reference/sql-query-builder: The SQL query builder builds typed queries from a table, with one method per SQL clause select() , innerJoin() , groupBy() , and the rest. It is closer to SQL than the ORM client is, and the same db gives you both. Reach for it when you need a join, aggregate, or SQL feature the ORM client doesn't expose, or when you want direct control over the generated SQL. Some methods work only on some databases, and some fail only when the query runs. For a task oriented guide to when and how to reach for the builder, see Advanced queries. note[The builder for SQL databases] The SQL query builder targets SQL databases; PostgreSQL and SQLite are supported today. MongoDB has no SQL builder use the ORM client for MongoDB queries, and the pipeline builder for aggregation pipelines. Example schema The examples run against the schema below and use the user , post , post tag , and tag tables. The grouped query examples use a separate customer and order schema, shown under Grouped queries. PostTag is the join table. The two list fields and the PostTag model together are how Prisma ORM 8 declares a many to many, which Relations and joins explains. For the schema syntax itself, see Contract authoring. Expand for the example schema Entry points In Prisma ORM 8 your schema.prisma is called contract.prisma . Coming from Prisma ORM 7 gets you from a Prisma ORM 7 project to that file, and has the rest of the setup steps. Install the client with npm install @prisma/orm postgres . Run npx prisma contract emit to write contract.json and contract.d.ts beside contract.prisma . The examples below assume your own file is in src/prisma/ , next to those two files, and they write the type import path as ./contract.d , exactly like that. You build queries from the client's sql property. Create a Postgres client with postgres(...) , then reach tables through db.sql.public . public is the PostgreSQL schema your tables are in. To put a model's table in another PostgreSQL schema, such as auth , wrap the model in a namespace auth { ... } block in your contract, and you then reach its table through db.sql.auth instead. See Namespaces. Table accessors are keyed by table name, not model name. A table name is the model's @@map value, or the model name exactly as written when the model has no @@map . In the example schema, the User model is mapped to user , so you write db.sql.public.user . The PostTag model for the join table is mapped to post tag , so you write db.sql.public.post tag . Column names are the field names unless a field sets @map , and for a field that does, you write the @map name everywhere in the builder. A field declared userId Uuid @map("user id") is select('user id') and f.user id , and each row you get back has a user id key. The db.sql builder [ the dbsql facet] A select() , insert() , update() , or delete() call starts a query. build() turns the chain into a query object, which the examples name plan . Nothing touches the database until you pass that object to db.query(...) or db.execute(...) . You can run the same built query more than once. To see the SQL without running it, pass it to db.toSql(...) . When your app shuts down, close the client with db.close() . The example schema's Embedding1536 column is a pgvector type, so a client for that schema also needs pgvector in extensions , as Built in functions shows. SQLite works the same way create the client with sqlite(...) from @prisma/orm sqlite/runtime . SQLite has no schemas, so there is no public in the path and the same table is db.sql.user . Of the SELECT methods on this page, lateralJoin() , outerLateralJoin() , and distinctOn() are not available on SQLite, but every other one is. The rest of this page shows PostgreSQL and writes the root as db.sql.public . Table access Every table on db.sql.public exposes the query building methods. Aliasing a query with .as() Call .as(alias) on a SELECT chain before build() to use that query as a subquery. The aliased query is then something you can pass to innerJoin() , outerLeftJoin() , and the other join methods. Do not call .as() inside a lateralJoin() callback. For the example, see Subquery via .as() . SELECT queries These methods build and refine a SELECT . They chain, and you resolve the query with build() followed by db.query(...) . Chain the methods in any order, with two exceptions a join must come before any call that names the joined table's columns, and the columns you pass to distinctOn() must be the first sort keys in orderBy() . SelectQuery in the tables below is the type they return. The set of column names a query can use is its scope it starts as the columns of the table you began with, and every join adds the joined table's columns to it. The where() , select() , orderBy() , update() , and other callback forms receive two arguments. The first is f , which has one property per column in scope. After a join, every column is on f under its table name, such as f.user.email or f.post.id . A column name that only one table has is also on f directly. The second is fns , an object of expression helpers such as fns.eq() and fns.raw . For an enum column you pass the value stored in the database, which is the string after = , so High = "high" is matched by fns.eq(f.priority, 'high') . A member with no = , such as admin in user type , is matched by its own name, fns.eq(f.kind, 'admin') . select() Reduce each row to a chosen set of columns or computed expressions. Options select() has three forms Form Signature Description Column names select('col', 'col2', ...) Keep the named columns. A name that is not in the query's scope throws an error whose code is ORM.COLUMN UNKNOWN . Aliased expression select(alias, (f, fns) = expr) Add one computed column under alias . Object of expressions select((f, fns) = ({ alias expr, ... })) Add several computed columns at once. The row type is inferred from the object's shape. Every form adds to what the query already returns calling select() a second time never replaces the first call's columns, whichever form you use. To return fewer columns, start a new query instead. A computed expression's result type comes from .returns(...) on fns.raw , or from the fns. function you called. Every fns.raw fragment needs .returns() . A type id is pg/ plus the PostgreSQL type name plus a version, always @1 today, such as pg/int4@1 or pg/uuid@1 . A few use a longer name that says what your code reads, such as pg/timestamptz date@1 for DateTime , read as a Date . The common ones are pg/text@1 , pg/int4@1 , pg/int8@1 , pg/float8@1 , pg/bool@1 , pg/uuid@1 , and pg/timestamptz date@1 . The full list is what your contract uses. Subquery via .as() Call .as(alias) on a SELECT chain before build() to use it as a subquery. Pass the result to any join method as the other argument. SELECT queries and grouped queries have .as() , but queries started with insert() , update() , or delete() do not, so you cannot join against the rows they return. Options Name Type Required Description alias string Yes Names the subquery. Address its columns as f. . after the join. Join it into an outer query first. Examples Join against a subquery Grouped queries Grouping starts with groupBy() , which turns a select query into a GroupedQuery . Write your aggregates in select() first, then call groupBy() . After that you can add having() , orderBy() , limit() , offset() , and distinct() . The examples below use an extra table, order , whose amount column is an integer groupBy() Group rows by one or more columns or by a computed expression, producing one row per distinct group. Use countBigInt() or sumBigInt(field) when totals can get that large. avg() is computed as a floating point number , so a long decimal is rounded. Use avgDecimal(field) when you need the exact figure. Every error this page names is an Error with a code property, so check for one as below. Group by a computed value Annotate with the type PostgreSQL computes, not the type you want. Here pg/numeric@1 types yearPlaced as string , which is what you receive, while .returns('pg/int4@1') would type it number and still hand you a string. .groupBy('yearPlaced') groups by the alias given to the selected value. To group by the expression itself, repeat the fragment inside groupBy() , .returns() and all A name that is neither a column of the table you started from nor an alias you selected throws an error whose code is ORM.COLUMN UNKNOWN , at the moment you call groupBy() . If you select a column you did not group or aggregate, the query fails when it runs, not when you build it, and that failure comes back as PostgreSQL's own error, not a Prisma ORM code. having() Filter groups by an aggregate comparison. Build the predicate from the aggregate functions ( fns.count , fns.sum , fns.avg , fns.min , fns.max ) and the comparison functions, comparing against a JavaScript literal. Remarks Compare against a plain JavaScript number, as in fns.gt(fns.count(), 1) . Passing a bigint literal such as 1n throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.ENCODE FAILED when the query runs. fns.countBigInt() and fns.sumBigInt() are the other way round compare those against a bigint literal, as in fns.gt(fns.countBigInt(), 1n) . Do not use a selected alias in having() . TypeScript will let you, but PostgreSQL rejects it and the query fails when it runs. Write the aggregate again instead.
