Mutations start from a table with insert() , update() , or delete() , and end with build() . Add returning() to get the affected rows back. Run a mutation with no returning() using db.execute(plan) , which resolves to { affectedRows } . With returning() , run it with db.query(plan) . The examples below go back to this page's example models, so they use db.sql.public.tag and db.sql.public.user again. insert() Insert one or more rows in a single statement. Remarks insert() always takes an array . A single row insert is a one element array. There is no separate single row overload. An empty array throws an error whose code is ORM.MUTATION DATA MISSING . Each row must include every column the database requires a column that is not nullable, has no @default(...) and is not generated on create. Leaving one out is a type error that names the column, such as Property 'displayName' is missing . A required column does not accept undefined either, so check a value typed T undefined before the insert. Before 8.0.0 rc.20 , such an insert compiled and then failed in the database. A column is optional when it is nullable, when it has a @default(...) (including now() and autoincrement() ), or when Prisma ORM generates it on create a field with @onCreate(...) , or typed by a named type that sets it, such as temporal.CreatedAt . Leave an optional column out and the database fills it from its default, or Prisma ORM generates it. Each row in one call is checked on its own, so rows may set different optional columns. Prisma ORM generates @onCreate(uuid()) values when you call build() , not when the query runs. The built query then holds fixed values, so running it twice inserts the same id twice, which fails on a unique column. Call .build() again for each insert. There is no ON CONFLICT and no upsert here. For "insert or update", use the ORM client's upsert() or write the statement with db.raw.sql . Options Name Type Required Description rows Array of row objects Yes The rows to insert. Each row requires the columns that are not nullable, have no default and are not generated on create; every other column is optional. Never call .returns() or param() on an insert value. Set columns with a values object, or derive new values from existing columns with an expression callback. Choose the rows with where() , and use returning() to get the updated rows. Form Signature Description Values object update({ col value, ... }) Set columns to fixed values. Expression callback update((f, fns) = ({ col expr })) Set columns to expressions computed from existing columns. Every value the callback returns must be an expression. To set a column to a fixed value in the callback form, wrap that value in a fns.raw fragment, as the second example below does. Remarks Import param from @prisma/orm postgres/relational core/expression . Values passed to insert() , update() , and comparison functions such as fns.eq(f.col, value) each take their type from the column they are used with, so you rarely need param() . Reach for it when the type the builder would pick is not the one the column needs. Inside fns.raw no column lends its type, so a bare string becomes pg/text@1 and a value compared there with a uuid column needs param(id, { codecId 'pg/uuid@1' }) . A Date or a Temporal.Instant cannot be interpolated bare at all. The option is called codecId , but it takes the same type id used everywhere else on this page. Binding a bare value with param() lists the type id each kind of JavaScript value gets, which is where to look for a date, a uuid, a boolean, or an array. Options Name Type Required Description value T Yes The value to bind. opts.codecId string Yes The type id to send the value as, for example 'pg/text@1' . Return type Return type Example Description ParamRef param('%@example.com', { codecId 'pg/text@1' }) A bound parameter reference usable inside fns.raw . Examples Bind a literal inside a raw fragment Expressions and functions Callback forms receive fns alongside the f argument. fns is an object of helper functions comparisons, boolean combinations, aggregates, and raw SQL. Built in functions These exist on every database Category Functions Comparison eq(a, b) , ne(a, b) , gt(a, b) , gte(a, b) , lt(a, b) , lte(a, b) Membership in(expr, values) , notIn(expr, values) Boolean and(...predicates) , or(...predicates) Existence exists(subquery) , notExists(subquery) Raw SQL raw ... .returns(typeId) For in() and notIn() , values is an array or a subquery. All four of in() , notIn() , exists() , and notExists() take a select query that you do not call build() on. Which aggregate functions exist depends on your database, and PostgreSQL gives you these eight. The contract type is the one you write in contract.prisma , and the PostgreSQL type is in brackets Function Returns count() / count(field) number . With no argument it counts rows. With a field it counts that field's non null values countBigInt() / countBigInt(field) bigint . Use it when the count can pass 2^53 1 sum(field) number over an Int ( int4 ) or BigInt ( int8 ) column. A string over Decimal ( numeric ), a number over Float ( float8 ) sumBigInt(field) bigint . The sum over an integer column that can pass 2^53 1 avg(field) number over an Int ( int4 ) or Float ( float8 ) column avgDecimal(field) An exact decimal string. The version of avg that does not round min(field) The input column's own type. A varchar column gives a String ( text ) max(field) The input column's own type. A varchar column gives a String ( text ) On PostgreSQL, fns also has ilike(expr, pattern) , a case insensitive SQL LIKE match for text columns, as in fns.ilike(f.displayName, '%alice%') . There is no fns.like , so write a case sensitive LIKE in a fns.raw fragment that returns a boolean ilike does not work on a native enum column, typed pg.enum(...) , because PostgreSQL cannot pattern match an enum type. Passing one is a type error. See Enums. Full text search on PostgreSQL uses fns.fullTextMatches(column, query) to filter, fns.fullTextRank(column, query) to score, and fns.fullTextHeadline(column, query) to return the matching text with each match marked. Build query from the search text with fns.websearchToTsquery(text) , fns.plaintoTsquery(text) , fns.phrasetoTsquery(text) , or fns.toTsquery(text) , or with the tsquery template tag from @prisma/orm postgres/target/full text . Never pass user input to fns.toTsquery() , because text that breaks PostgreSQL's search syntax makes the query fail when it runs; use fns.websearchToTsquery() or the tsquery tag for user input. Full text search on the ORM client reference explains what each of these does, and the index that lets PostgreSQL search without reading every row. To search a @@fullTextIndex , pass the index from the table's indexes in place of the column fns.fullTextMatches(post.indexes.post search, q) and fns.fullTextRank(post.indexes.post search, q) , where post is db.sql.public.post . The query reads the index's fields, weights and language from the contract, so it searches every field of a weighted index and PostgreSQL uses the index. To search several columns that no index covers, build the search document with fullTextDocument from @prisma/orm postgres/target/full text . Each of the three full text functions takes an options object as its last argument, and each accepts language . Pass the same language to the function that builds query , as in fns.fullTextMatches(f.title, fns.websearchToTsquery(q, { language 'german' }), { language 'german' }) . fullTextRank also takes normalization and coverDensity , which the ORM client reference describes. fullTextHeadline also takes these options startSel and stopSel the text put before and after each match. PostgreSQL uses and when you leave them out. maxWords and minWords the longest and shortest headline, in words. minWords must be lower than maxWords . highlightAll true return the whole text with every match marked, instead of a short excerpt around the matches. This query returns each matching post with its rank and a headline that marks the matches with rank is a number , and a higher rank is a better match. headline is a string the title with each match between and . pgvector is the PostgreSQL extension for vector columns. If your contract uses a pgvector type, such as Embedding1536 in the example schema, pass pgvector in extensions when you create the client, because without it postgres(...) throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.MISSING EXTENSION PACK fns then also has fns.cosineDistance(a, b) , which returns the cosine distance between two vectors as a number . Each argument is a vector column or an array of numbers, as in fns.cosineDistance(f.embedding, queryEmbedding) . See Extension types. fns.raw and .returns() Write a raw SQL fragment as a tagged template, and interpolate columns, typed expressions, and bare JavaScript values with ${...} . For a bare value, the builder picks the type id from its JavaScript type. Binding a bare value with param() lists which JavaScript type becomes which type id, and shows how to choose a different one with param(...) . Call .returns(typeId) to declare the fragment's result type. Options Name Type Required Description SQL fragment Tagged template
reference/pipeline-builder: The pipeline builder gives you a typed way to build MongoDB aggregation pipelines. You reach it through db.query , chain aggregation stages onto a starting collection, and finish the chain with the call that builds the query. It is the MongoDB counterpart to the SQL query builder a lower level API for the queries the ORM client doesn't express. Everything the builder produces becomes a MongoDB aggregation pipeline. There is no find() or distinct() here, so use db.orm or rawCommand() for those. To fetch a single document, filter and then limit(1) . Use the ORM client ( db.orm ) for everyday reads and writes across models and relations. Reach for the pipeline builder when you need to group documents, to join another collection and keep transforming the result, or to write the result into a collection ( $out and $merge ). This page documents every stage, accumulator, expression helper, and write method. note[This is the MongoDB pipeline builder] The pipeline builder targets MongoDB only. PostgreSQL has no pipeline builder use the SQL query builder for PostgreSQL joins and aggregates, and the ORM client for everyday queries on either database. Example schema The examples run against the schema below, the same MongoDB schema as the ORM client page. Article and Tutorial are two kinds of Post , stored in one posts collection and told apart by the value of the kind field. @@base(Post, "article") and @@discriminator(kind) set that up. See @@base on the ORM client page. @@type("mongo/string@1") says the enum is stored as a MongoDB string, and @1 is the version of that type id, always @1 today. None of that matters to a pipeline kind is an ordinary field you can filter and group on. Expand for the example schema Entry points Every pipeline starts with db.query.from('posts') , naming the collection to aggregate over. It ends with a call that turns the chain into a query you can run, and between them you chain stages. db is the client you create with mongo(...) , whose dbName option is the name of the MongoDB database to use. See Transactions and runtime for every option and for how to create the client. Three Prisma ORM import paths appear on this page @prisma/orm mongo/runtime holds the mongo() client, @prisma/orm mongo/query builder holds mongoQuery , fn , acc , and expr , and @prisma/orm mongo/query ast/execution holds the Mongo Stage classes, MongoAggFieldRef , and MongoFieldFilter . Every example holds the built query in a variable named plan . Prisma ORM 8 renames schema.prisma to contract.prisma . Run npx prisma contract emit before any code on this page compiles it writes contract.json , used at run time, and contract.d.ts , used for types. The example below imports contract.json with with { type 'json' } , which works with the TypeScript settings prisma orm init writes for you. Coming from Prisma ORM 7 has the setup steps. from() Enter the pipeline builder on a collection. Remarks from() takes the collection name, the same name you use on db.orm ( 'posts' , 'users' ), not the model name Post . The collection name is the model's @@map value, or the model name exactly as written when there is no @@map . Passing an unknown collection name throws right away, with an error whose code is ORM.MODEL UNKNOWN and whose message is Unknown root " ". Valid roots ... (the message says root; it means the collection name). from() returns a builder you chain stages onto. Call insertOne() and insertMany() on from() directly, before any stage. reference/raw-queries: Raw queries are the way out when the typed APIs can't express the query you need. Reach for a typed API first the ORM client for everyday reads and writes, the SQL query builder for PostgreSQL joins and aggregates, and the pipeline builder for MongoDB aggregation. When none of them reaches the SQL clause or MongoDB command you need, drop down to raw. There are two kinds of raw query PostgreSQL raw SQL (the fns.raw tagged template for fragments and the db.raw.sql tag for whole statements) and MongoDB raw commands ( db.raw.collection(...) and db.query.rawCommand(...) ). PostgreSQL raw SQL Raw SQL comes in two forms. A raw fragment is a piece of SQL you put inside a builder query. Write it as a tagged template with fns.raw and pass it to a select() , where() , orderBy() , or update() call. The rest of the query stays typed. A whole raw statement is a complete SQL statement written with db.raw.sql . It takes the place of $queryRaw and $executeRaw from Prisma ORM 7. If it returns rows, as a $queryRaw query did, end it with .returnsRow(spec).build() , where the spec is a column list defined below, and pass the result to db.query(...) . If it does not, as with $executeRaw , end it with .affectedCount().build() and pass the result to db.execute(...) . To see the SQL a built query would send, without running it, pass it to db.toSql(...) . warning[Only .returnsRow() converts values for you] A type id such as pg/text@1 tells Prisma ORM what JavaScript type a column should become, and the property is named codecId . .returnsRow(spec) names a type id for every column of a whole db.raw.sql statement, so you get real JavaScript values back. A fragment's .returns(...) does not convert anything it only tells TypeScript what type to expect, so the value is whatever the pg package, the PostgreSQL driver underneath, gives you. For a text or an integer column that is already a JavaScript string or number, while a numeric column arrives as a string. A date column gets no conversion by Prisma ORM, so you get the pg package's own value for that column. The examples in this section run against the user / post schema from the SQL query builder page. See its example schema for the full model definitions. As on that page, create the client with postgres(...) and reach tables through db.sql.public , which is keyed by table name (the model name exactly as written, unless the model sets the @@map attribute, which renames a table). db.query(...) and db.execute(...) run a built query. fns.raw in a projection A projection is the select() list. A select() callback receives two arguments f , with one property per column, and fns , with the expression helpers. fns.raw is a tagged template. Write a SQL fragment, interpolate columns and values with ${...} , and declare the fragment's result type with .returns(typeId) . See select() for every form it accepts. .returns(...) only tells TypeScript what to expect it does not cast the value in SQL and it does not change how the pg package reads it. It takes a type id string, or an object of the form { codecId, nullable } . See Binding a bare value with param() for the type ids you are most likely to write, and the SQL query builder's fns.raw and .returns() for the full treatment. fns.raw as a where() predicate where() 's callback returns a boolean expression, the same thing the comparison helpers such as fns.eq(...) return. A raw fragment that declares .returns('pg/bool@1') is itself a boolean expression, so you can pass it straight to where() without wrapping it in fns.eq(...) . Interpolating a typed expression You can interpolate another expression, such as a comparison, a column reference, or another raw fragment. The expression itself goes into the fragment, not its rendered SQL, so it stays type checked. An interpolated value is sent as a query parameter, never pasted into the SQL. A column or table name cannot be interpolated as a string, because a string becomes a parameter. When the column is chosen at run time, pick it in your own code from a fixed set of columns you control, and choose the matching fns.raw fragment or select() call for each one. Binding a bare value with param() Interpolate a plain number , string , boolean , bigint , or Uint8Array directly. For anything else, such as a point in time or a decimal you want stored as numeric , wrap the value in param(value, { codecId }) and name the type id yourself. Import param from @prisma/orm postgres/relational core/expression . A bare value that you do interpolate directly gets the type id Prisma ORM picks from its JavaScript type The value you interpolate The type id it gets a whole number from 2147483648 to 2147483647 pg/int4@1 a larger whole number , up to 9007199254740991 pg/int8number@1 , which reads back as a number any other number , including a fractional one pg/float8@1 a bigint pg/int8@1 , which reads back as a bigint a string pg/text@1 a boolean pg/bool@1 a Uint8Array pg/bytea@1 A type id is pg/ , a name, and @1 . The name is usually the PostgreSQL type, and a few carry a suffix that says which JavaScript type you get, such as pg/int8number@1 for a number , pg/timestamptz date@1 for a Date and pg/timestamptz temporal@1 for a Temporal.Instant . Between those two, pick pg/int8@1 when the value can exceed 2^53. Three more you are likely to write are pg/uuid@1 , pg/numeric@1 , and pg/jsonb@1 . Those are the common ones, not the whole set. For any column, db.sql.public. .columns. .codecId is its id, and the same ids are in contract.json under storage.namespaces. .entries.table. .columns. .codecId . A point in time is the case param() exists for pg/timestamptz date@1 takes a Date , and pg/timestamptz temporal@1 takes a Temporal.Instant , which needs a global Temporal , as Supported versions shows. Declaring a nullable result The object form of .returns() declares a nullable result. Use it when a fragment can evaluate to SQL NULL , so the result type is T null . The client level db.raw.sql tag db.raw is the client's raw API, beside db.sql and db.orm . On PostgreSQL it holds sql , the same tagged template as fns.raw . On MongoDB it holds collection(...) instead, which the MongoDB raw commands section covers. Unlike fns.raw , db.raw.sql works outside a builder callback, and it has the extra methods that turn a whole statement into a query you can run. Use .returns(...) to build an expression ahead of time and pass it to the object form of select() , which names each output column Use .returnsRow(spec) to run a whole statement and get converted rows back. The spec names the columns of every returned row, and each entry is either a column from your contract or a type id. A column such as db.sql.public.user.columns.id brings its own conversion, nullability, and TypeScript type. Write a type id for a column your contract has no match for, and the object form { codecId 'pg/text@1', nullable true } when that column can be NULL , as a LEFT JOIN column can. If a returned row has no column your spec names, the query throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.RAW ROW COLUMN MISSING . A failing statement throws a SqlQueryError whose sqlState is the PostgreSQL error code for the failure, such as 23505 for a unique constraint violation. Use .affectedCount() , which takes no spec, for a statement that returns no rows. Pass the built query to db.execute(...) , which resolves to { affectedRows } , the number of rows the statement changed. You can also run a built raw query inside a transaction db.transaction() gives you a tx , and tx.query(...) and tx.execute(...) take the same built queries as db.query(...) and db.execute(...) do. You can nest a .returnsRow() query inside another that is how you write a subquery or a CTE, which is a WITH query. Interpolate it before .build() , and call .build() on the outer one only. Its .returns property holds its declared columns, so outer.returnsRow({ postCount inner.returns.postCount }) reuses a declaration. You cannot nest a statement that ends with .affectedCount() , because it produces no rows. You can nest an UPDATE ... RETURNING , because it does. note[Three names look alike] .returns(typeId) is a method on a fragment, .returnsRow(spec) is a method on a statement, and .returns is a property on the object .returnsRow() gives you. Unsupported interpolation Interpolation accepts columns, expressions, param(...) values, raw queries that return rows, and the bare types number , bigint , string , boolean , and Uint8Array . Interpolating anything else, such as a Date , is rejected by TypeScript when you compile. In plain JavaScript the tagged template throws as soon as you call it, with an error whose code is RUNTIME.RAW SQL UNSUPPORTED INTERPOLATION and this message To bind any value whose type is not in the list, wrap it in param(value, { codecId }) with the right type id. For a Date , use pg/timestamptz date@1 . MongoDB raw commands db.raw.collection(collectionName) returns an object with nine methods for running MongoDB commands directly against a collection. The collection name is the one your contract declares ( 'users' , 'posts' ), the same name the ORM client uses ( db.orm.users ). MongoDB has no schemas, so there is no public segment here and none on db.orm . There is no raw find() , so use aggregate () with a $match stage. MongoDB has no transactions in Prisma ORM, so a raw command cannot run inside one. See Transactions (MongoDB). Each of these nine methods builds a command call .build() on it, then run it with runtime.query(...) , where runtime is what await db.runtime() returns. This is true of the writes too. A write returns a one element array, so destructure it with const [result] = ... . An update or delete command can also run with runtime.execute(...) , which resolves to { affectedRows } . You cannot run a command with db.query(...) as you would on PostgreSQL, because on MongoDB db.query is the pipeline builder, which builds aggregation pipelines. warning[MongoDB raw results are native BSON values] Nothing on the MongoDB side of this page is converted for you. Raw commands name fields as they are stored in the database, so a field the ORM calls id because it is declared id ObjectId @id @map(" id") is id here, in filters and in the rows you get back. An id comes back as it is stored one that MongoDB generated is an ObjectId instance from the mongodb package, the MongoDB driver underneath, not a hex string. Compare one with String(row. id) === aliceId . Raw filters take native BSON values too, so build ids with that package's ObjectId class. The write methods give you the counts and ids under the mongodb package's own key names, { insertedId } , { matchedCount, modifiedCount, upsertedCount, upsertedId } , and { deletedCount } , and you read those keys directly. The examples in this section run against the users / posts schema from the pipeline builder page. See its example schema for the full model definitions. Create the client with mongo(...) , get the connection that runs a built query from await db.runtime() , and declare the two example ids once aggregate () Run a raw aggregation pipeline against a collection. The type parameter says what each returned row looks like. The pipeline stages are raw MongoDB documents, sent as you wrote them, so a filter on id with a real ObjectId matches. insertOne() and insertMany() Insert one or many documents. Both return the mongodb package's own insert result, with ObjectId instances for the generated ids. insertMany() 's insertedIds is a plain array of ObjectId , in the order you passed the documents. updateOne() and updateMany() Update one or every matching document. The first argument is a raw filter document, and the second is either an update document such as { $set ... } or an aggregation pipeline, which is an array of stages. Both return { matchedCount, modifiedCount, upsertedCount, upsertedId } . Update document form Pipeline form An array update is a full aggregation pipeline update, so a stage can reference the document's other fields. deleteOne() and deleteMany() Delete one or every matching document. Both return { deletedCount } . findOneAndUpdate() Atomically update a matching document and return the document as it was before the update. When no document matches and upsert is true , the update inserts one. Remarks findOneAndUpdate() accepts only { upsert } as its third argument. It cannot sort, and it cannot give you the document as it is after the update. TypeScript rejects sort or returnDocument in the options object. To sort, or to read the document after the update, build the command yourself and run it through db.query.rawCommand(...) . new RawFindOneAndUpdateCommand(...) takes six arguments collection the collection name. Required. filter the filter document. Required. update an update document, or an array of aggregation pipeline stages. Required. upsert a boolean. Optional, and false when you leave it out. sort a record of field name to 1 or 1 . Optional. returnDocument 'before' or 'after' . Optional. Leave it out and you get the document as it was before the update. Upsert counter pattern findOneAndUpdate() returns the document as it was before your update. The first call creates the document, so there is nothing to return and you get [] . The second call returns count 1 , which is the value before that call added one. The example schema has no counter collection, so users stands in for one here. MongoDB allows a plain string id , so 'pageViews' is a valid id. The advice to build ids with ObjectId applies to ids MongoDB generated. findOneAndDelete() Atomically delete a matching document and return it. The yielded row is the raw matched document itself, not a wrapper object, so its id is a raw ObjectId . db.query.rawCommand() db.query.rawCommand(command) runs a raw MongoDB command, sent exactly as you wrote it. See the pipeline builder. It returns a built query already, so do not call .build() on it. Unlike aggregate () it has no row type parameter, so its rows come back as unknown and you cast them yourself. rawCommand() is the way out when the typed pipeline builder can't express a query. The command you pass is sent unchanged, so a real ObjectId in a pipeline document matches. aggregate () on db.raw.collection() handles id filtering too, and it gives you a row type, so use rawCommand() when you are already working in db.query and need one raw command there. For the full treatment see the pipeline builder's rawCommand() section.
reference/transactions-and-runtime: Create, connect, and close the client, run transactions, prepare statements, and set per query execution options, on PostgreSQL and MongoDB. For a task oriented walkthrough, see the Fundamentals guide to Transactions. For the ways to query inside a transaction, see the ORM client reference, the SQL query builder reference, and the raw queries reference. If you are coming from Prisma ORM 7, your schema.prisma is now called contract.prisma . Running npx prisma contract emit writes two files next to it contract.json , which your app imports, and contract.d.ts , which gives you the TypeScript types. A new project keeps all three files in src/prisma/ . Every client you create needs the contract from contract.json , turned into a value with contractFromJson . A query such as prisma.user.findMany({ where }) is now db.orm.public.User.where(...).all() . Coming from Prisma ORM 7 lists the packages to install, the commands to run, and the rest of the renamed calls. db is the client that postgres(...) or mongo(...) returns. db.runtime() gives you the object that actually runs queries, and that object is called the runtime. Transactions are not available on MongoDB. To run one there, pass your own MongoClient with the mongoClient option and use the driver's session.withTransaction(...) , which Transactions on MongoDB shows in code. Client lifecycle on PostgreSQL Create a PostgreSQL client with postgres(...) , connect it to get a runtime, run queries, and close it when you are done. postgres(options) Create a PostgreSQL client. Remarks Pass the contract as a value with the contract option. Turn contract.json into that value once with contractFromJson (contractJson) from @prisma/orm postgres/static , as every example below does. Contract is the type that contract.d.ts exports; you name it here because TypeScript cannot read a type out of a JSON file. The client takes its types for db.orm and db.sql from the value, so postgres(...) takes no type argument. If you write your contract in TypeScript with defineContract instead of in contract.prisma , what defineContract returns is already a contract value, so pass it as contract directly. contractFromJson checks the contract once. Build every client from the same value, and export it from the module that creates the client so that tests and other modules can import it. Tell the client which database to use in one of three ways url , pg , or binding . A binding wraps any of the three choices in one object, with a kind field saying which it is { kind 'url', url } , { kind 'pgPool', pool } , or { kind 'pgClient', client } . Use it when your code picks the source at run time. Pass exactly one of url , pg , and binding , or leave all three out and pass one to connect() . postgres(...) checks the database input when you call it, and a wrong one throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.BINDING INVALID at once, not on the first query. The message names the option. A url , top level or in a binding , must be a non empty string that starts with postgres // or postgresql // ; an empty one does not fall back to the PG environment variables or to localhost. A pg value must be a pg.Pool or a pg.Client . A binding must have the kind 'url' , 'pgPool' or 'pgClient' , and its pool or client must be an object. null as url , pg or binding fails too, even beside another input, so leave out an option that has no value instead of passing null ts title="src/prisma/db.ts (excerpt)" const url = process.env['DATABASE URL']; const db = postgres({ contract, ...(url === undefined ? {} { url }) }); supabase(...) from @prisma/orm extension supabase/runtime checks its database input the same way, but takes no pg.Client , because each role bound query needs a connection of its own. A pg.Client , as pg or as a binding with kind 'pgClient' , fails with an error whose code is SUPABASE.CONFIG INVALID . supabase(...) checks only that the pool of a { kind 'pgPool', pool } binding is an object, so make sure it is a pg.Pool . When you pass a pg pool or client, directly or as a binding with kind 'pgPool' or kind 'pgClient' , you own it call db.close() first, then close it yourself with pool.end() for a pool or client.end() for a client. db.close() closes the client's runtime but leaves your pool or client open. The driver sets DateStyle to ISO on each connection of a pool or client you pass, before first use, so do not change DateStyle on those connections a date or time read under another style fails with RUNTIME.DATE STYLE NOT ISO . When you pass a url , the client creates the pool and closes it. Set that pool's timeouts with poolOptions , which has no effect on a pool you supply yourself. Some types come from a PostgreSQL extension, such as a pgvector.Vector(1536) type in your contract.prisma . Run npm install @prisma/orm extension pgvector first. Then import pgvector from '@prisma/orm extension pgvector/runtime' and pass extensions [pgvector] . A middleware is an object with a name and one or more hooks, such as { name 'no big deletes', beforeEncode (plan) = { if (plan.sql.includes('DELETE')) throw new Error('blocked') } } . Throw from a hook to block the statement. Prisma ORM runs every statement and transaction as an activity the lifecycle hooks are activityStarted , activityEnded , and activityFinalized , and the hooks that change or stop a statement are beforeCompile , beforeEncode , intercept.onQuery , intercept.onExecute , and onRow . See How middleware works. Migrations record in your database which contract it matches. With verifyMarker 'onFirstUse' , the default, the first query checks that record and logs a warning on a mismatch, then runs anyway. If you see the warning, run npx prisma db update . verifyMarker false skips the check. postgres(options) does not open a connection. The client opens one on first use, so connect() is optional call it to open the connection up front and fail early. Without cursor , a read loads its whole result before it gives you the first row. With cursor { batchSize 100 } , reads go through a server side cursor and fetch the rows in batches of that size, so a for await loop gets the first rows before the rest arrive. cursor {} uses batches of 100. A batchSize that is not a positive integer makes postgres(...) throw an error whose code is RUNTIME.ARGUMENT INVALID . While a for await loop reads through a cursor, the cursor holds its database connection until the loop ends. A query inside the loop that needs the same connection waits forever. That happens when you loop over a query on a transaction's tx and query tx inside the loop, and on a client you created with one pg Client . Options Pass exactly one of url , pg , and binding . Name Type Required Description contract Contract value Yes The contract, from contractFromJson (contractJson) or defineContract . url string See note A PostgreSQL connection string. pg Pool or Client from the pg package See note An existing pg instance to use. You close it yourself. binding { kind 'url' \ 'pgPool' \ 'pgClient', ... } See note The same three choices in one object. poolOptions { connectionTimeoutMillis? number; idleTimeoutMillis? number } No Timeouts for the pool the client creates from url (defaults 20000 / 30000 ). extensions Array of extension runtimes, the default export of each package's /runtime subpath No The PostgreSQL extensions your contract's types need. Install each package, then import its /runtime subpath and put the default export in this array. middleware Array of middleware No Code that runs around every query. See How middleware works. verifyMarker 'onFirstUse' or false No Whether the first query checks that the database was set up for this contract. Defaults to 'onFirstUse' . log An object with info , warn , and error methods, such as console No Where the client reports what it does not throw a 'warn' result from the lints or budgets middleware, the verifyMarker warning about a missing or mismatched contract marker, such as CONTRACT.MARKER MISSING , and errors from middleware hooks it cannot pass to your code. Without log , these are not printed. postgresServerless() , sqlite() and supabase() take it too. cursor PostgresCursorOptions , which is { batchSize? number } No Read through a server side cursor in batches of batchSize rows, 100 when you leave batchSize out. Without cursor , reads are not batched. mode 'strict' or 'permissive' No How middleware treats a rule violation. Defaults to 'strict' . See mode . collections Object mapping model name to a collection class No Your own collection classes, used on db.orm and on every transaction's tx.orm . See Custom collections. The type of the options object is PostgresOptions , exported from @prisma/orm postgres/runtime . Return type Return type Example Description PostgresClient postgres({ contract, url }) A client that has not connected yet. Its members are listed below. .orm holds your models by model name. See the ORM client reference. .sql is the SQL query builder, keyed by PostgreSQL schema, then by table name db.sql.public.tag . The table name is the model's @@map value, or the model name exactly as written when the model sets no @@map . See the SQL query builder reference. Write raw SQL with db.raw.sql ... , as the raw queries reference shows. .enums holds the enum values from your contract, by PostgreSQL schema db.enums.public.Role . Each member is the value a query returns, such as a bigint for a member of a 64 bit integer enum, so has() , nameOf() , and ordinalOf() find a value read from the database that equals a member. .nativeEnums holds only the values of enum types that exist in PostgreSQL itself, created with CREATE TYPE from a native enum block or nativeEnum() , also by schema. An enum block or enumType() is not listed there; read it through .enums . Look the type up by name in brackets db.nativeEnums.auth['AalLevel'].values is ['aal1', 'aal2', 'aal3'] . .contract is the contract as an object. connect() , runtime() , query() and execute() , toSql() , transaction() , prepare() , and close() are documented on this page. Examples Create a client from a connection string These examples assume the file is beside contract.json in src/prisma/ , so from anywhere else, change the relative paths. Write ./contract.d exactly like that, with no extension. It resolves under preserve or esnext with bundler , the settings prisma orm init writes, and under nodenext as CommonJS; under nodenext , node18 , or node20 as ES modules it does not, and the upgrade guide covers that case. The line import contractJson from './contract.json' with { type 'json' } needs Node.js 22.18 or newer and TypeScript 5.9 or newer. In tsconfig.json it needs resolveJsonModule true and one of these module settings, each with its moduleResolution preserve with bundler , esnext with bundler , or nodenext with nodenext . node18 and node20 also work, with moduleResolution left unset. prisma orm init writes preserve and bundler into new projects. When module is nodenext and package.json has no "type" "module" , TypeScript treats the file as CommonJS, and there the import is import contractJson from './contract.json'; with no with part. The Prisma ORM 7 to 8 upgrade guide walks through which setting fits which kind of project. TypeScript types every process.env value as possibly undefined, so the examples write ! after it, the same way prisma orm init does. Bind to an existing pg pool connect() Open a connection and return a runtime. Remarks Returns a Promise . The runtime is the connected object that runs queries. It has these calls runtime.query(built) runs a built query and returns its rows. A built query is the object you get from .build() at the end of a builder or raw chain. See Running a built query. runtime.execute(built) runs a built query that returns no rows, such as an insert, and returns { affectedRows } . See Running a built query. runtime.connection() takes one connection out of the pool so that several queries run on the same connection. It returns a promise, and you put the connection back with connection.release() const connection = await runtime.connection(); try { await connection.query(built) } finally { await connection.release() } . See Manual connection and transaction control. runtime.prepare(declaration, callback) prepares a statement you run many times with different values. The client has a prepare() too, and the two do the same thing. See Prepared statements (PostgreSQL). runtime.telemetry() reports how the most recent query went. See runtime.telemetry() . connect() takes the same database options as postgres(...) , so a client you created without one can be given its database here await db.connect({ url process.env.DATABASE URL! }) , or await db.connect({ binding { kind 'url', url } }) . Every error has a code property, and the error reference lists them all. Catch the error and compare error.code with the value shown here, for example if (error.code === 'DRIVER.NOT CONNECTED') . You rarely need connect() running a query connects the client. connect() without options is safe to call at any time, also after a query or a second time it waits for a connection in progress, or resolves with the runtime the client's queries already use. connect(options) on a client that is already connected rejects with an error whose code is DRIVER.ALREADY CONNECTED and whose message is Postgres client is already bound . A connect() still waiting when you call close() rejects with DRIVER.NOT CONNECTED . Return type Return type Example Description Promise const runtime = await db.connect() The connected runtime. Examples Connect and run a query runtime() Get the current runtime synchronously. Remarks On PostgreSQL, runtime() is synchronous it returns the Runtime directly, not a promise. You can call it before connecting, because the client connects on first use. Return type Return type Example Description Runtime const runtime = db.runtime() The runtime, returned synchronously. db.query(plan) and db.execute(plan) [ run a plan] Run a built query on the client. Remarks db.query(plan) runs a built query and returns its rows as an AsyncIterableResult . db.execute(plan) runs a built query that returns no rows and resolves to { affectedRows } . They do what db.runtime().query(plan) and db.runtime().execute(plan) do, so you do not need the runtime to run a query. Both take RuntimeExecuteOptions as a second argument. A transaction's tx , a serverless connection, and SQLite's sqlite(...) client have the same two members. Keep db.runtime() for connection() and telemetry() . Examples Run a SQL builder query and a raw write db.toSql(plan) Render a built query as the SQL it would send, without running it. Remarks Returns { sql, params } . params holds the query's values before Prisma ORM converts them for the database. toSql() needs no database. It works on a client created with no url , pg , or binding , on the serverless client, on a transaction's tx , and on the static context from @prisma/orm postgres/static . It takes a query from db.sql , db.raw , or the ORM. Middleware does not run, so changes a beforeCompile hook would make are not in the result. A query built for prepare() , with parameters in it, throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.PREPARE BIND ON ADHOC . A query built from another contract throws PLAN.HASH MISMATCH . Running either query throws the same errors. Return type Return type Example Description { sql string; params readonly unknown[] } db.toSql(plan) The SQL text and its parameter values. Examples Print the SQL of a query mode The mode option says how middleware treats a rule violation. Remarks Of the built in middleware, only budgets reads mode . The lints middleware sends a rule set to 'warn' to log.warn in either mode. 'strict' , the default, makes the budgets middleware throw on every violation. With 'permissive' , a budgets violation whose severity is 'warn' is passed to log.warn , where log is the log option you pass to the client, such as log console , and the query runs. Without a log option, the warning goes nowhere. Set the severity with the budgets severities option. A violation whose severity is 'error' still throws. postgres(...) , postgresServerless(...) , sqlite(...) , and supabase(...) take mode . Its type is RuntimeMode . Examples Log budget warnings instead of throwing close() Close the client and release its pool. Remarks Returns a Promise . close() replaces $disconnect() from Prisma ORM 7. You can call it more than once; calls after the first do nothing. A closed client cannot be used again. After close() , connect() rejects and runtime() throws an error whose code is DRIVER.NOT CONNECTED ( Postgres client is closed ). db.query(...) , db.execute(...) , db.transaction(...) , db.prepare(...) , and ORM calls such as db.orm.public.User.all() report the same error through what they return the promise rejects, or the result rejects when you await or read it. They do not throw at the call, so a try / catch catches the error only when you await the call. Create a new client with postgres(options) if you need one. Queries already running when you call close() finish first. close() also closes the client's runtime, so a runtime you got from db.runtime() before close() refuses new work with DRIVER.NOT CONNECTED ( Runtime is closed ). When you created the client from your own pg pool or client, close() leaves that pool or client open; call await pool.end() after it. In a server, call close() when the process receives SIGTERM or SIGINT , and never in a request handler, because every request shares the pool. Stop the server first, so that no new query starts, then close the client. app is your Express app and db is the client from src/prisma/db.ts . Once both are closed, Node.js exits by itself; if it does not, something else, such as another database client or a timer, is still open A script that runs once, such as a seed, calls await db.close() at the end. Without it, the open pool keeps the process running until its idle connections time out, 30 seconds by default ( poolOptions.idleTimeoutMillis ). Return type Return type Example Description Promise await db.close() Resolves when the client is closed. Examples Close when finished await using (automatic disposal) The client implements Symbol.asyncDispose , so await using closes it automatically at the end of its block. Remarks Disposal fires at the end of the block the await using declaration lives in, not on the next line. Scope the client to the block where you need it. After the block exits, the client is closed the same way close() closes it a later connect() rejects with an error whose code is DRIVER.NOT CONNECTED . await using needs @types/node installed, or "esnext.disposable" added to the lib array in your tsconfig.json . Examples Close automatically with await using Serverless client on PostgreSQL @prisma/orm postgres/serverless exports postgresServerless , a client for serverless and edge runtimes such as Cloudflare Workers, AWS Lambda, and Vercel. It holds no database connection, so you create it once, outside your request handler. Each request opens its own connection with connect({ url }) . postgresServerless(options) Create a serverless client. Remarks It takes the options of postgres(...) that say how queries run contract , extensions , middleware , log , verifyMarker , cursor , mode , and collections . The type of its options object is PostgresServerlessOptions . It takes no database options. You pass the connection string to connect() instead. It has sql , raw , enums , nativeEnums , contract , and toSql() , which need no connection, and connect() . It has no orm , runtime() , or transaction() . Those are on the connection. As on postgres(...) , reads load the whole result unless you pass cursor . Behind Cloudflare Hyperdrive, reads through a cursor hang, so leave cursor out there. connect({ url }) on the serverless client Open a database connection and return it. Remarks Returns a Promise . The connection has the members of a postgres(...) client except connect() orm , sql , raw , enums , nativeEnums , contract , runtime() , query() , execute() , toSql() , transaction() , prepare() , and close() . The collection classes you passed as collections are on its orm . Code written for a postgres(...) client works on it. Import the type PostgresServerlessConnection from @prisma/orm postgres/serverless . connect() opens the connection before it returns. It rejects with an error whose code is DRIVER.CONNECTION FAILED when the database refuses the connection, rejects the credentials, or does not answer within 20 seconds, and it leaves nothing open. A URL that does not start with postgres // or postgresql // makes it reject with RUNTIME.BINDING INVALID . Close the connection with await using , as the example below does, or with close() . Await every query before the connection closes. A query whose rows you read after that fails. Each connection that connect() returns uses one database connection. While a for await loop reads through a cursor, a query on the same connection inside the loop waits forever. Examples Query from a Cloudflare Worker Client lifecycle on MongoDB Create a MongoDB client with mongo(...) . The entry point and several lifecycle details differ from PostgreSQL, most notably that runtime() is asynchronous. mongo(options) Create a MongoDB client. Remarks Pass the contract as a value with the contract option, the same way as on PostgreSQL. Import contractFromJson from @prisma/orm mongo/static and build the value with contractFromJson (contractJson) . The type of the options object is MongoOptions . Tell the client which database to use in one of four ways url , uri , mongoClient , or binding . A binding wraps the choices in one object, with a kind field saying which it is { kind 'url', url, dbName } or { kind 'mongoClient', client, dbName } . Use it when your code picks the source at run time, and use the url kind for a uri . Pass exactly one of the four, or leave all four out and pass one to MongoDB connect() . dbName is separate and does not count as one of the four, so { url, dbName } is allowed. With url , the database name comes from the path of the connection string, as in mongodb //host 27017/app . Add dbName to override that name, or when the string has no name in its path. uri takes the same kind of string, and always needs dbName . Client ownership with url or uri , Prisma ORM creates the underlying MongoClient and closes it on close() . With mongoClient , you supplied the client, so Prisma ORM does not close it. Because close() leaves your client open, you can use one MongoClient both through Prisma ORM and in code you write against the mongodb package directly. You close that client yourself. mongo(options) does not open a connection. The runtime is built on first use, or explicitly via MongoDB connect() . A contract built with extension packs records them under extensions in contract.json , so pass the runtime of each pack the contract records to the extensions option, as on PostgreSQL mongo({ contract, url, extensions [myPack] }) , with myPack imported from the pack's /runtime subpath. When a pack the contract needs is missing, mongo(...) throws an error whose code is RUNTIME.MISSING EXTENSION PACK . Options Pass exactly one of url , uri , mongoClient , and binding . dbName is separate, and uri and mongoClient both require it. Name Type Required Description contract Contract value Yes The contract, from contractFromJson (contractJson) or defineContract . url string See note A mongodb // or mongodb+srv // string, with the database name in its path. uri + dbName string + string See note The same kind of string, plus the database name, which is required here. mongoClient + dbName MongoClient + string See note An existing MongoClient you own, plus the database name. binding { kind 'url' \ 'mongoClient', ... } See note The same choices in one object. extensions Array of extension runtimes, the default export of each pack's /runtime subpath When the contract records extension packs The extension packs your contract was built with. Without one of them, mongo(...) throws RUNTIME.MISSING EXTENSION PACK . middleware Array of middleware No Code that runs around every query. See How middleware works. mode 'strict' or 'permissive' No Defaults to 'strict' . Prisma ORM ignores this value. It is passed through to your middleware so your own code can branch on it. Return type Return type Example Description MongoClient mongo({ contract, url, dbName }) A client that has not connected yet. MongoClient here is Prisma ORM's own type, exported from @prisma/orm mongo/runtime . The mongodb driver has a class with the same name, so in a file that imports both, rename one of them in its import import type { MongoClient as PrismaMongoClient } from '@prisma/orm mongo/runtime' . .orm holds your models by collection name, with no .public in the path db.orm.users . The collection name is the model's @@map value, or the model name exactly as written when the model sets no @@map . The example schema sets @@map("users") on User , which is why the key here is users . See the ORM client reference. .query is the pipeline builder, which builds MongoDB aggregation pipelines. See the pipeline builder reference. .raw sends raw MongoDB commands. See the raw queries reference. .enums holds the enum values from your contract, and .contract is the contract as an object. MongoDB connect() , MongoDB runtime() , and MongoDB close() are documented below. Examples Create a client from a connection string Share an existing MongoClient connect() Open a connection and return a runtime. Remarks Returns a Promise . You rarely need connect() running a query connects the client. connect() without options is safe to call at any time, also after a query or a second time it waits for a connection in progress, or resolves with the runtime the client's queries already use. connect(options) on a client that is already connected rejects with an error whose code is DRIVER.ALREADY CONNECTED and whose message is Mongo client is already bound . A connect() still waiting when you call close() rejects with DRIVER.NOT CONNECTED . connect() takes the same database options as mongo(...) , so a client you created without one can be given its database here await db.connect({ url process.env.MONGODB URL!, dbName 'app' }) . Return type Return type Example Description Promise const runtime = await db.connect() The connected runtime ( query , execute , and close only). runtime() Get the runtime. Remarks On MongoDB, runtime() returns a Promise you must await it. PostgreSQL's runtime() is synchronous, so write await db.runtime() on MongoDB and db.runtime() on PostgreSQL. MongoRuntime has query , execute , and close only. It has no connection() , prepare() , or telemetry() . See Transactions (MongoDB) and Execution options and results. Return type Return type Example Description Promise const runtime = await db.runtime() The runtime, resolved asynchronously. runtime.query() Run a built query through the runtime. Remarks (await db.runtime()).query(built) runs any built MongoDB query, including one built by the pipeline builder ( db.query ). Returns an AsyncIterableResult , which holds the rows the query returns await it for an array, or for await to read the rows one at a time as they arrive. For an update or delete command, use runtime.execute(built) , which returns { affectedRows } . Other commands throw an error whose code is RUNTIME.MONGO STATISTICS UNSUPPORTED . There is no execute() on the client itself. Return type Return type Example Description AsyncIterableResult await (await db.runtime()).query(built) The built query's rows. Examples Run a query built by the pipeline builder [ run a pipeline builder plan] close() Close the client. Remarks Always call db.close() . runtime.close() leaves the client looking open, and later calls fail. Returns a Promise . After close() , any further use rejects with an error whose code is DRIVER.NOT CONNECTED ( Mongo client is closed ). That covers db.runtime() and ORM access such as db.orm.users.first() , since both go through the same runtime. When you supplied a mongoClient , close() does not close your client (see mongo(options) ). Return type Return type Example Description Promise await db.close() Resolves when the client is closed. Examples Use after close throws await using (automatic disposal) The MongoDB client implements Symbol.asyncDispose too, so await using closes it at the end of its block. Remarks Disposal fires at the end of the block, exactly as on PostgreSQL. After the block exits, a later connect() rejects with an error whose code is DRIVER.NOT CONNECTED . Examples Close automatically with await using Transactions (PostgreSQL) A transaction groups several writes into one unit they all commit together, or they all roll back. Use db.transaction(...) in application code. If you are writing a function that takes a runtime as a parameter instead of the client, use withTransaction(...) . If you need to run several statements on one connection, get a connection with runtime.connection() and call commit() or rollback() yourself. db.transaction(callback) Run a callback inside a transaction. The transaction commits when the callback returns and rolls back when it throws. Remarks Query through tx , not db . tx has the client's query members orm , sql , raw , prepare , query , execute , and toSql . tx.orm holds your models, with your custom collection classes if you passed any. Build queries with tx.sql or tx.raw , then run them with tx.query(...) to get rows back, or tx.execute(...) when the write returns no rows. tx.execute(...) resolves to { affectedRows } , the number of rows the statement changed. Every call on tx uses the same transaction connection, and queries on db run outside the transaction. db.transaction(...) takes the callback and nothing else. reference/migration-api: Each migration is its own folder inside migrations/app/ , and the file you edit in it is migration.ts . app is the fixed name of the folder that holds your project's migrations; extension packages that ship their own migrations get folders of their own next to it. In Prisma ORM 8, schema.prisma is now contract.prisma , your contract the same language and the same models. npx prisma migration plan writes migration.ts from a change to the contract, and saves a frozen copy of the contract for the migration to point at; when this page says a migration's start or end contract, it means one of those copies. You edit migration.ts , then run it with Node.js, and it writes ops.json , the SQL that will run, next to itself. npx prisma db migrate applies ops.json to the database. This page lists everything migration.ts can call. For the editing workflow, with a worked backfill, read Editing a migration. On PostgreSQL, everything comes from one module migration plan writes the import line with only the names the migration needs. When you add a call by hand, add its name to the import line. Where a migration holds SQL from your contract, such as a default, a check or an index expression, migration plan writes it as a sql value, as in fn(sql clock timestamp() ) , imported from the same module. Every call that takes SQL accepts either a sql value or a plain string. A string is used exactly as written, while a sql value has its shared indentation and the blank lines at its start and end removed, so leave the strings in a migration you already applied as they are. On MongoDB the module is @prisma/orm mongo/target/migration ; the path really does contain target , and it is not a placeholder. See MongoDB operations. The migration file migration.ts exports one class that extends Migration . This is what migration plan writes for a migration that adds one column The four imports at the top point at snapshots, which are copies of your contract that migration plan saves under migrations/snapshots/ / one for the contract the migration starts from and one for the contract it ends at. You never type those paths; migration plan writes them. codecRef on the column names how its values are read and written; leave it as migration plan wrote it. The last line is what makes the file runnable with Node.js; keep it as written. Member What it is Migration The base class. Start and End are the two snapshots' types. startContractJson The start snapshot's contract.json . endContractJson The end snapshot's contract.json . operations The list of changes. They run in the order you list them, table changes and data changes alike, so a dataTransform between two column changes runs between them. Each entry is one call to a method or helper on this page. Return the list as it is; do not await the calls. this.endContract A read only view of the end contract, for looking up names and settings in your own code. this.endContract.namespace.public.table.user is the user table in the public schema ( namespace in that path means the PostgreSQL schema). this.startContract The same for the start contract, or null on a first migration. A first migration starts from an empty database, so it has no start snapshot. migration plan writes it as extends Migration , without the two Start imports and without startContractJson . Running the file turns operations into ops.json , and also writes migration.json , which records the start and end contracts. Every Node.js version Prisma ORM supports (22.18 or newer on the 22 line, 24.11 or newer on the 24 line, or 26 or newer) runs the .ts file directly, with no build step. It reads the prisma.config.ts that owns the migration, to learn which database and extensions the project uses the nearest one above the migration's directory whose migrations directory holds the file, else the one in the working directory, or the one you pass with config . It never connects to a database. Flag What it does dry run Prints migration.json and ops.json to the terminal instead of writing them. config Reads that config file instead of ./prisma.config.ts . help Prints the flags. Any other flag fails with an error whose code is CLI.UNKNOWN FLAG . Operation classes and checks Every operation carries an operationClass , which says what kind of change it makes. The methods below set it for you, and rawSql asks you for it. The class changes nothing about what runs npx prisma db migrate applies every class, and marks each destructive operation with ⚠ and a data loss warning. Class Meaning Example additive Adds something new Add a column, create an index widening Loosens a rule, or renames something without losing anything Drop NOT NULL , rename an index destructive Removes or changes something that exists, and can lose data Drop a column, change a column's type data Changes rows, not tables A dataTransform Most operations also carry two check queries, a precheck and a postcheck, and db migrate runs them in this order 1. The postcheck, which asks "is the change already there?". If it passes, the operation is skipped. This is what lets you run db migrate again after a run stopped partway what already landed is skipped. 2. The precheck, which asks "is the database in the state this change expects?". If it fails, the run stops. 3. The statements. 4. The postcheck again. If it fails now, the run stops. The methods below write both checks for you; you write them yourself only in rawSql . How migrations work has the full rule. PostgreSQL operations Each operation is a method you call on the migration, this. ({ ... }) , with one options object. Every method takes schema ; a schema? in the tables below means you may leave it out. For createSchema , renameSchema and dropSchema it is the schema to create, rename or drop. For every other method it is the PostgreSQL schema the table is in, which is public unless your contract sets another. Names are quoted for you pass user , not "user" . Pass the table name, which is the model name exactly as written, such as User , unless the model sets @@map a model with @@map("user") has the table user . Runs is the SQL for this page's example names. Schemas and tables Method Options Runs Class createSchema schema CREATE SCHEMA IF NOT EXISTS "app" additive createTable schema , table , columns , constraints? CREATE TABLE "public"."post" (...) additive renameTable schema? , table , to ALTER TABLE "public"."userProfile" RENAME TO "UserProfile" widening dropTable schema , table DROP TABLE "public"."post" destructive renameSchema schema , to ALTER SCHEMA "billing" RENAME TO "finance" widening setTableSchema schema? , table , to ALTER TABLE "public"."invoice" SET SCHEMA "billing" widening dropSchema schema DROP SCHEMA "billing" widening columns is a list of col(...) calls and constraints a list of primaryKey(...) , unique(...) , foreignKey(...) , and checkExpression(...) calls, all rendered inside the CREATE TABLE statement. That section shows a full createTable call and the SQL it produces. renameTable renames a table and keeps its rows. It also renames each primary key, unique constraint, foreign key, index and check whose name migration plan derived from the old table name, so it returns a list of operations spread it into the list, as in ...this.renameTable({ table 'userProfile', to 'UserProfile' }) . It reads the names from the migration's start and end contracts. Change the table name in your contract (the model name, or its @@map ), and run prisma contract emit . migration plan plans the change as a dropped table and a new one replace that pair with the renameTable call, or write the call in an empty migration from prisma migration new . Pass schema only when more than one schema has a table of that name. When the start contract has no such table, or the end contract has no table named to , it fails with MIGRATION.TABLE RENAME UNMATCHED . On SQLite, renameTable takes table and to . renameSchema renames a schema, and everything in it stays in it. setTableSchema moves a table to the schema to , with its rows, constraints, indexes and policies; foreign keys from other tables keep pointing at it. Leave out schema for a table that is in no schema. Later renameTable and renameColumn calls in the same migration find the table under its new schema or schema name. dropSchema drops a schema without CASCADE , so drop or move its tables first its precheck fails while the schema still holds a table, view, sequence, type or function. migration plan writes these calls when you pass rename billing finance , rename public.Invoice billing.Invoice or delete billing . They are PostgreSQL only. Columns Method Options Runs Class addColumn schema , table , column ALTER TABLE "public"."user" ADD COLUMN "bio" text additive dropColumn schema , table , column ALTER TABLE "public"."user" DROP COLUMN "bio" destructive alterColumnType schema , table , column , type , using? , raw? , operationClass? ALTER TABLE "public"."post" ALTER COLUMN "views" TYPE bigint destructive, or data with using setNotNull schema , table , column ALTER TABLE "public"."post" ALTER COLUMN "views" SET NOT NULL widening dropNotNull schema , table , column ALTER TABLE "public"."post" ALTER COLUMN "views" DROP NOT NULL widening setDefault schema , table , column ALTER TABLE "public"."user" ALTER COLUMN "name" SET DEFAULT 'anonymous' additive, or widening when the column already has a default dropDefault schema , table , column ALTER TABLE "public"."user" ALTER COLUMN "name" DROP DEFAULT widening addColumn and setDefault take a col(...) call as column . The other methods take the column's name as a string. alterColumnType takes the new type in type , written the way a migration writes it, such as 'int8' , 'varchar(255)' , or '"Mood"' for an enum. Prisma ORM recognizes the PostgreSQL types it supports and the types of the extension packages in your configuration, and after the change db migrate checks that the column has the type you wrote. A type it does not recognize fails with MIGRATION.COLUMN TYPE UNREADABLE . If that type comes from an extension package, add the package to your configuration. For any other type, set raw true and pass the type exactly as PostgreSQL prints it, because db migrate then compares the column's type with that text. using is the expression in the USING clause, for a conversion PostgreSQL cannot do on its own. Without it, the column is cast to the new type. Write it as SQL over the column, such as '"views" bigint' . A semicolon, a SQL comment or dollar quoting outside a quoted literal, or a comma or a keyword such as FROM outside parentheses, fails with MIGRATION.SQL EXPRESSION INVALID . The operation is data when it has a using , and destructive otherwise; pass operationClass ( 'widening' , 'destructive' , or 'data' ) to choose another class. When the column is an autoincrement() column, alterColumnType also changes the sequence the column owns to the new width, with ALTER SEQUENCE ... AS bigint for an int8 column. It first refuses, before any statement runs, when the sequence has already handed out a value too large for the new width. A migration applied before 8.0.0 rc.19 left the sequence at its old width. Change it yourself, for example ALTER SEQUENCE "public"."post id seq" AS bigint ; pg get serial sequence('"public"."post"', 'id') names the sequence. A using needs a type change. If the new type is the type the column already has in the contract the migration starts from, migration.ts refuses the alterColumnType with MIGRATION.ALTER COLUMN TYPE USING WITHOUT TYPE CHANGE , because db migrate would find that the column already has that type and skip the operation, so the conversion would never run. To change the values in a column and keep its type, write a dataTransform instead, which checks the rows themselves. A migration.ts written before 8.0.0 rc.18 passed an options object with qualifiedTargetType , formatTypeExpected and rawTargetTypeForLabel . It now stops with MIGRATION.OPERATION OPTION REMOVED move qualifiedTargetType to type and options.using to using , and delete the other two. If no database has applied the migration yet, run it again to write ops.json ; if one has, leave ops.json and migration.json as they are, because writing them again changes the migration's hash. setDefault takes the column with its new default, and Prisma ORM writes the DEFAULT clause column col('name', 'text', { default lit('anonymous'), codecRef { codecId 'pg/text@1' } }) , or column col('createdAt', 'timestamptz', { default fn('now()') }) . When you pass a codecRef , Prisma ORM first checks that a literal default is a valid value of that type, and a value that is not fails with CONTRACT.DEFAULT INVALID . setDefault has no postcheck, so it always runs, which means it can also replace a default the column already has. After the last operation, db migrate checks that the default matches your contract. The operation is widening when the column already has a default in the contract the migration starts from, and additive otherwise. setDefault takes no operationClass ; a call that still passes one runs and ignores it. A migration.ts written before 8.0.0 rc.15 that still passes defaultSql stops with MIGRATION.OPERATION OPTION REMOVED , so rewrite the call as shown above. Its existing ops.json still applies. setNotNull has an extra precheck that fails while the column still holds a NULL , so backfill the column with a dataTransform first. Editing a migration shows the three steps. Pass its kind as kind , one of 'primaryKey' , 'unique' , or 'foreignKey' . kind is recorded in ops.json for reporting only and does not change the SQL; it defaults to 'unique' . A check constraint has its own dropCheckConstraint . addCheckConstraint adds a check to a table that already exists; checkExpression(...) , listed under helpers, is the same thing inside a createTable . In both, expression is SQL and goes into the statement as you wrote it, so quote column names yourself 'length("title") 0' . There is no method that renames a column. Raw SQL shows a column rename. To rename a table, use renameTable . Indexes Method Options Runs Class createIndex schema , table , index , columns or expression , extras? CREATE INDEX "post author idx" ON "public"."post" ("authorId") additive renameIndex schema , table , from , to ALTER INDEX "public"."post author idx" RENAME TO "post author id idx" widening dropIndex schema , table , index DROP INDEX "public"."post author id idx" destructive createIndex takes either columns , a list of column names, or expression , one SQL string that becomes everything between the parentheses, such as 'lower("title")' . Everything else goes in extras Field What it is unique true for CREATE UNIQUE INDEX . where The partial index condition, as SQL, without the WHERE keyword. type The index method 'gin' renders USING "gin" . options Index storage parameters as an object { fastupdate false } renders WITH ("fastupdate" = off) . With many true , the column is a list, and the value is replaced in or removed from every list that holds it. Values are passed as parameters, in the form the column stores them. codecRef names the column's codec, and enumValue names the enum member, so that a failed check names it; migration plan fills in both.
